The Colossians were being urged to give religious devotion to angelic beings — to venerate them as mediators and guardians of the cosmic order, channels through which one might safely approach God. (Some read the phrase as joining in the worship the angels offer in the heavenly realm, claimed by the visionaries; either way, angels are given a place that belongs to Christ alone.) The error is plain: it dethrones the one Mediator between God and men (1 Tim. 2:5) and bows to the very powers that Christ is head over (2:10). Angels themselves will not allow it — when John fell down to worship one, the angel refused: “You must not do that…worship God” (Rev. 19:10).

“Going on in detail about visions” — the third strand. The false teacher paraded “the things he had seen” — mystical visions and supernatural experiences gained through his disciplines (the word behind “going on in” may be a technical term for an initiate “entering” the inner sanctuary). He took his stand on these experiences, dwelt on them, built his authority from them: “I have seen things you have not; I have access to the heavenly realm; follow me, and you can too.” It was spiritual one-upmanship by experience — making private revelations, rather than Christ and his Word, the measure of who is truly advanced.

“Puffed up without reason by his sensuous mind” — Paul’s verdict. Now Paul lances the whole thing. For all its impressive display, the man is simply “puffed up” — swollen, inflated with pride — and “without reason,” groundlessly: there is nothing actually there. And the killing stroke: he is puffed up “by his sensuous mind” — literally, “the mind of his flesh.” Here is the irony at the heart of it. The man who beats his body to escape the flesh, who scales the heavens in visions to rise above it, is in fact being driven the whole time by the flesh — by the fallen nature’s craving for status, recognition, and superiority. The austerity feeds his pride; the visions feed his self-importance; his “humility” is vanity in disguise. It is all about self — animated not by the Spirit of God but by the flesh wearing spiritual dress.

What might these strands be today? All three are still with us. Asceticism reappears wherever holiness is equated with severity — extreme diets or fasts worn as spiritual medals, a grim legalism that measures godliness by how much one denies oneself, the quiet assumption that the harder I am on myself the holier I must be. Angel-veneration resurfaces in the modern fascination with angels, “spirit guides,” and cosmic “energies,” and, within the church, in every tendency to slip other mediators — saints, special “anointed” figures — between the believer and Christ. Visionary one-upmanship lives on in the experience-chasing that rates a Christian by whether he has had dramatic encounters, special revelations, or ecstatic experiences, and in the leader who builds a following on his private visions rather than on Christ and Scripture. Beneath all of them runs the same two-part error Paul named: a spiritual elite making ordinary believers feel disqualified unless they add some extra practice or experience to Christ — and, underneath the impressive show, the same fleshly pride. The safeguard, in every age, is the next verse: hold fast to the Head. cf. 1 Cor. 8:1; Col. 2:23.

verseByVerse.quote: and not holding fast to the Head, from whom the whole body, nourished and knit together through its joints and ligaments, grows with a growth that is from God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Not holding fast to the Head” — what did Paul have in mind? “Holding fast” means to grip tightly, to cling, to keep a firm hold. And “the Head” is Christ (as in 1:18 and 2:10). So here, in five words, is Paul’s diagnosis of the entire heresy: for all his visions and disciplines and angel-talk, the false teacher has let go of Christ. He has shifted his grip — from the Saviour to rules, experiences, and spiritual beings. And that is fatal, because everything depends on keeping hold of the Head. It is the exact opposite of the healthy Christian Paul described a few verses back, “rooted and built up in him” (2:7). Note too what the word implies: the believer is called actively to hold on — not to drift, not to loosen his grip when something newer and more impressive comes along. Anything that draws your hand off Christ to grasp something extra is pulling you away from the only One who gives life.

“From whom the whole body…grows” — the metaphor. Christ is the Head; the church is his body. And from the Head — and from nowhere else — the whole body draws its life. Paul fills in the anatomy: the body is “nourished” (supplied, fed) and “knit together” (joined, bound into one) “through its joints and ligaments” — the connecting tissues that both link the parts to one another and carry the supply down from the head to every limb. The picture is of life flowing from Christ the Head, through all the connections, into every member, so that the body is at once fed and held together — and therefore grows. And the growth, Paul says, “is from God”: the increase is God’s own doing, his gift, not something the body manufactures by its own effort or technique (cf. Eph. 4:15–16; 1 Cor. 3:6–7). Real growth comes down from the Head; it is never worked up from below.

So that Old Joe gets it. Here is the whole thing in a picture. Cut a branch from the vine, and it does not grow — it withers and dies, because all the life was in the vine (John 15:5). Sever a hand from the arm, and no amount of exercise will make it grow; it is finished the moment it is cut off. That is exactly what the false teachers were unwittingly doing: by drawing people off Christ onto their rules and visions, they were cutting the branch from the vine — offering a fancier life while severing it from its only source. So two things for Old Joe. First, his spiritual growth is not a technique he must master; it is the natural fruit of staying joined to Jesus. His job is to hold fast to the Head — to keep close to Christ in faith, in the Word, in prayer — and God himself supplies the growth. Stop hunting for life in programs and experiences and rule-keeping; stay gripped to Christ, and you will grow, because the life flows from him. Second, he does not grow alone: he grows as part of the body, knit to other believers, the life of the Head running through the connections. A Christian was never meant to be a severed limb. Hold fast to the Head, stay joined to the body, and leave the growing to God.

verseByVerse.quote: If with Christ you died to the elemental spirits of the world, why, as if you were still alive in the world, do you submit to regulations — ‘Do not handle, Do not taste, Do not touch’…? These have indeed an appearance of wisdom in promoting self-made religion and asceticism and severity to the body, but they are of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“If with Christ you died to the elemental spirits of the world” — what does this mean? The “if” is not a doubt but a settled fact: since you died with Christ. The “elemental spirits” (stoicheia, as in v. 8) are the basic governing principles and powers of the old order — the whole system of religious rules and the spiritual forces behind it, the ABCs of a world running apart from Christ. And Paul says you died to all of it. United to Christ in his death (2:11–12), you were severed from that old regime, released from its jurisdiction — for death dissolves every old bond and obligation (Rom. 7:1–6). The elemental rules have no more claim on you than a master has on a slave who has died.

“As if you were still alive in the world” — but were they not alive? Alive, yes — physically, they were breathing and walking about. But they had died, with Christ, to “the world” in Paul’s sense: the old order organized apart from God, the realm of the elemental rules. So to take up that world’s regulations again is to behave “as if” they still belonged to it — as if the death had never happened, as if they were still under its sway and owed it obedience. Paul calls it submitting to “regulations” (literally, letting yourself be decreed at). It is a freed slave voluntarily walking back into the slave-quarters and picking up his old chains. Why, Paul presses, would a dead-and-risen people live by the rule-book they were freed from?

“Do not handle, Do not taste, Do not touch” — the regulations themselves. Paul quotes the slogans of the system, and notice their character: every one is a prohibition — don’t, don’t, don’t. A religion of forbiddings, fussing over contact with certain foods and objects. The rules even pile up pettily — “touch” is lighter than “handle,” so that even the faintest contact is banned. This is the asceticism of v. 18 reduced to its bumper-sticker slogans, and Paul lets their narrowness speak for itself.

“Things that all perish as they are used” — the deflation. In a quiet aside Paul lets the air out of the whole system: the things these rules agonize over — foods and the like — are perishable. They “perish as they are used”: eaten, consumed, passed through the body, and gone. They cannot touch the soul (the Lord said as much — what enters the stomach does not defile the heart, Mark 7:18–19). Why would anyone build his standing before God on rules about things destined for the rubbish heap?

“According to human precepts and teachings” — where the rules come from. Here is the decisive stroke: these regulations are man-made. They are “human precepts and teachings,” not the commands of God — the very phrase the Lord Jesus flung at the Pharisees, quoting Isaiah: “teaching as doctrines the commandments of men” (Mark 7:7; Isa. 29:13). And that settles their authority over the conscience: none. Rules God never gave cannot bind a soul God has freed.

“An appearance of wisdom” — why they are so attractive. Paul grants it: these things “have indeed an appearance of wisdom.” They look wise — rigorous, profound, deeply spiritual. The fasting looks like serious devotion; the strict rules look like holiness; the severity looks like depth. That is exactly their danger: it is a reputation of wisdom, a convincing surface, with no reality beneath. The most dangerous religion is always the kind that looks most like the real thing.

“Self-made religion and asceticism and severity to the body” — what that surface trades on. Three things give the system its impressive look. Self-made religion translates a word Paul coins here and which appears nowhere else in all of Greek — ethelothrēskia, “will-worship”: worship a man chooses for himself, devotion springing from human will rather than from God’s command. Asceticism is the show of “humility” again (as v. 18). And severity to the body (literally “unsparingness”) is harsh, merciless treatment of the body — punishing the flesh to prove one’s seriousness. Self-chosen worship, paraded humility, bodily rigour: it is a religion that looks magnificent. But Paul’s coined word exposes its root — it is self-will dressed up as devotion, religion invented by man rather than revealed by God.

“Of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh” — the verdict that brings it all down. For all the impressive show, the whole system fails at the one thing it claims to do: it cannot actually curb sin. External prohibition does not conquer the flesh; it only relocates it. Starve the body, and the flesh does not die — it grows fat on pride, swelling with self-righteous satisfaction in its own discipline. The man who renounces certain foods to subdue his flesh simply finds his flesh feeding on the conquest. Rules can trim outward behaviour, but they cannot change a heart, and they may even inflame the very sin they forbid (Rom. 7:5–8). The flesh is not defeated by a rule-book; it is defeated only by death and resurrection with Christ — which is exactly where Paul turns next (3:1–5).

The whole passage, for Old Joe. Here is Paul’s point in plain words. You died with Christ to the old world of rule-keeping, so do not crawl back under man-made religious rules as though you still belonged to it. Such rules — don’t handle, don’t taste, don’t touch — look wise and holy and rigorous, and they are dangerously attractive. But three things are wrong with them: they are invented by men, not given by God; they fuss over perishable, material things that cannot touch the soul; and — the fatal flaw — they have no power whatever to make Old Joe holy. They are like cutting weeds off at ground level: the garden looks tidy for a day, but the roots are alive and the weeds come straight back. Only Christ digs out the root. So Old Joe must not measure his walk with God by a list of don’ts, and must not let a strict, impressive, self-denying religion fool him into thinking it can change his heart. The cure for sin is not a tighter rule-book; it is a living Saviour. He has died and been raised with Christ — so the way forward is not to climb back under the rules, but to hold fast to the Head and live the new life from above, which is precisely what chapter 3 will now unfold. cf. Rom. 8:13; Gal. 5:16.

3.title: Set Your Minds on Things Above: The Old and the New
3.overview:
Chapter 3 is the ethical consequence of everything chapters 1–2 have established. The logic is characteristically Pauline: because of who you are in Christ (indicative), live accordingly (imperative). You have died with Christ; you have been raised with Christ; your life is hidden with Christ in God; Christ is your life. Therefore: set your minds on things above, put to death what is earthly in you, put off the old self, put on the new self — and let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, the word of Christ dwell in you richly, and everything you do be done in the name of the Lord Jesus.

The chapter’s structure is the structure of the gospel applied to daily life: the negative movement of putting off (vv. 5–11), and the positive movement of putting on (vv. 12–17). The things to be put off are the practices of the old self — sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, covetousness, anger, wrath, malice, slander, obscene talk, lying. The things to be put on are the character of the new self — compassion, kindness, humility, meekness, patience, forbearing one another, forgiving each other, and above all, love, which binds everything together in perfect harmony.

The chapter then extends this transformation into the household (vv. 18–4:1): the practical ordering of the most intimate human relationships — wives and husbands, children and fathers, slaves and masters — under the lordship of Christ. These are not arbitrary social regulations; they are the gospel working its way into the fabric of daily life, the supremacy of Christ (chapter 1) arriving at the breakfast table, the bedroom, and the workplace.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Set Your Minds on Things Above
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Chapter 3 turns from what the believer must not do (the rule-religion demolished in chapter 2) to a wholly new direction. “If then you have been raised with Christ” — and the “if” means “since”: the resurrection with Christ is an accomplished fact. The believer has already been raised, here and now — he need not climb a single rung through fasting, visions, or angels to reach the heavenly realm, for in Christ he is already there. From that ground come two commands that reach the whole inner person: seek the things above (the bent of desire and pursuit) and set the mind on them (the settled orientation of thought). This is no mystical escapism that despises the body, the job, or the home — it is the reordering of the entire life around the risen, reigning Christ, the way an exile lives and works in a foreign land with his heart fixed on home, for “our citizenship is in heaven.”

And the things above are not the celestial geography of the false teachers; they are wherever Christ is — “seated at the right hand of God,” the place of supreme honour and finished work, the very powers the Colossians feared now beneath his feet. The crucified one is the crowned one, and he reigns there as the believer’s own representative and advocate. Why seek what is above? Because that is where the believer’s true life now is: “you have died” (the old self buried with Christ) and “your life is hidden with Christ in God” — at once safe, locked in the most secure place in the universe, beyond the reach of any enemy, and hidden, not yet on display.

For the hiddenness has an appointed end. “When Christ who is your life appears” — he does not merely give life; he is our life — “then you also will appear with him in glory.” The ordinary, unremarkable believer, like an heir who has lived his whole life unrecognised, will be led out and revealed in glory beside the King on the day of his coming. That certain future is the great motive for present holiness, and it carries the whole section that follows.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Hidden Life and the Security of the Believer in Christ

Colossians 3:3 — “your life is hidden with Christ in God” — is one of the New Testament’s most comprehensive statements of the security of the believer. The life of the Christian is not exposed to the attacks of the world, the flesh, or the devil in any ultimate sense; it is hidden, concealed, kept safe in the most secure location possible: with Christ, in God. Reformed theology has always grounded assurance of salvation not in the believer’s performance but in the security of their position: in Christ, kept by God. This is why the Christian can face the world’s hostility and the flesh’s internal rebellion without ultimate despair; the life that matters is in a place nothing can reach.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossians were being told that their spiritual security depended on correct navigation of the angelic hierarchy, proper observance of festivals and food laws, and achievement of special spiritual states. Paul says: your life is hidden with Christ in God. There is no spiritual power that can reach it; no ritual failure that can revoke it; no ignorance of esoteric knowledge that can diminish it. Now: The Christian whose sense of security rises and falls with their spiritual performance — who feels secure on days of devotional discipline and insecure on days of failure — needs to hear this: your life is hidden. It is not at risk. It is kept by the one whose power infinitely exceeds every force that would threaten it.

verseByVerse.quote: If then you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“If then” — the turn of the argument. All through chapter 2 Paul has been pulling down the rule-bound, ascetic religion of the false teachers, ending with the verdict that such things are powerless to deal with sin (2:20–23). Now he gives the positive alternative. He has been working with two halves of one truth: in 2:20 he said, “if you died with Christ…why submit to regulations?” — the death-with-Christ that frees you from the world’s rules. Here he takes the other half: “if then you have been raised with Christ…seek the things above.” The point is decisive: the cure for a failed religion of rules is not no effort and no direction, but a new direction. Not down into severity to the body, but up toward the risen Christ. The Christian life is not asceticism; it is aspiration — the whole self reaching upward to where Christ is.

Does Paul mean “if” — or “since”? He means since. The little word (ei) here does not raise a doubt about whether the Colossians have really been raised with Christ; it reasons from the fact that they have. It is the same construction as 2:20. We could fairly translate, “Since you have indeed been raised with Christ…” Paul is not asking his readers to wonder whether they belong to Christ; he is building his command on the solid ground that they do.

“Raised with Christ” — pause and wonder. This is not a promise about the distant future; it is a statement about what has already happened. United to Christ (2:12), the believer shares his resurrection — now. The same almighty power that rolled the stone away and brought Jesus out of the tomb has raised Old Joe to new life. He is not waiting to be made alive someday; in Christ he is already as truly raised as his Lord is raised, because his Lord’s resurrection is his own. The grave is behind him; the new creation has already begun in him. And see how completely this answers the heresy: the false teachers urged the Colossians to climb — through fasting, through visions, through angels — to reach the heavenly realm. Paul says they need not climb a single rung. In Christ they have already been raised there. cf. Eph. 2:5–6.

“Seek the things that are above” — what does that mean? “Seek” is a present command — keep on seeking. To seek a thing is to pursue it, to set your desire and effort on it, to make it your aim and your treasure. And “the things above” are the realities of the realm where Christ reigns — his kingdom, his values, his priorities. But Old Joe may be puzzled, so let us say plainly what this does not mean. It does not mean floating about in mystical detachment, despising his job, his family, or his daily life — that would be the very escapism and asceticism Paul has just condemned. It is not a new set of rules, nor merely daydreaming about heaven. What it means is the reorientation of the whole bent of his life — his desires, aims, treasure, and ambition — around the risen Christ and his everlasting kingdom, rather than around the passing things of earth. The man who seeks the things above still drives his van and pays his bills; but he does it all for Christ and aimed at Christ’s kingdom, not as the be-all of his existence. It is a matter of what he is finally living for. “Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matt. 6:21): to seek is to set the heart’s compass to point up.

“Where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God” — why does Paul add this? He locates “the things above” with precision: they are where Christ is, and Christ is at God’s right hand. In the Bible the right hand of God is the place of supreme honour, of all authority and dominion, and of finished work — for Christ sat down there, his saving work complete (Ps. 110:1; Heb. 1:3; 10:12). Paul presses this for the comfort packed into it. The Christ Old Joe is told to seek is no dead teacher and no distant ideal; he is the living, enthroned Lord of the universe, seated at the centre of all power — and the very powers the false teachers feared lie beneath his feet (2:10, 15). And now let it land: the same Jesus who hung on the cross bearing Old Joe’s debt is now seated on the throne of heaven, ruling all things — the crucified one is the crowned one. The carpenter of Nazareth, the man of sorrows, sits at God’s right hand in glory; and he is yours, reigning there as your representative and your advocate (Rom. 8:34). To seek the things above is to seek him — and he could not be more secure, more powerful, or more entirely for you.

verseByVerse.quote: Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Set your minds on things that are above.” Verse 2 deepens verse 1. There Paul said “seek” (pursue, with desire and effort); here he says “set your minds” — another present, ongoing command. The word means more than passing thought; it is the settled bent of the mind, the whole orientation of one’s thinking, caring, and valuing (the same word as “have this mind among yourselves,” Phil. 2:5). What you habitually dwell on, ponder, and prize — set that on the things above, on the risen Christ and his kingdom. The seeking of verse 1 flows from a mind set there: aim the thoughts upward, and the life will follow.

“Not on things that are on earth.” And here is the deliberate counterweight. The mind is not to be set on “things on earth” — not the earthly, perishable things treated as ultimate: the possessions, status, and priorities of the old order (the perishable things of 2:22, and the very sins he is about to list in 3:5, which he calls “what is earthly in you”). The two cannot both be the mind’s true north at once. Whichever a man fixes his mind on will shape him: a mind set on earth makes an earthbound man; a mind set above makes a heavenly-hearted one. cf. Rom. 8:5–6; Phil. 3:19–20.

So that Old Joe understands it rightly. This is easy to take the wrong way, so let us be clear. “Set your mind on things above” does not mean Old Joe should become so heavenly-minded he is no earthly good; it does not mean despising the world, his body, his work, or honest pleasures (that is the asceticism Paul just demolished); and it does not mean drifting through life in a mystical haze. Of course Old Joe must still think about his job, his bills, and his garden — that is right and godly, and Paul will give him very down-to-earth instructions about home and work in just a few verses. The question is what his mind is finally set on: what he treasures, what governs him, what he interprets all of life by. Think of an Englishman living and working abroad: he does his job and pays his way in the foreign country, but his heart is set on home — his citizenship, his family, his future are there, and everything he does is coloured by where he truly belongs. So it is with the Christian: “our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20). Old Joe lives and labours on earth with his heart set on home — on Christ, and the kingdom that will never perish. To fill the mind with Christ — his Word, his promises, his reign — and to view every earthly thing in that light: that is setting the mind on things above.

verseByVerse.quote: For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“For” — the ground beneath the command. Why should Old Joe seek and set his mind on the things above? Paul gives the reason: “for you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.” The command rests on a fact about who he now is. His very life is located above, with Christ — so of course he should seek what is above, where his life actually is. And the two truths of the new self are now complete: he has been raised with Christ (v. 1), so he reaches upward; and he has died (v. 3), so the old earthbound life is behind him.

“You have died.” This is a finished fact (the tense points to a completed act): in union with Christ’s death, the old Old Joe — the self that belonged to the world and was ruled by its principles — has died and been buried with Christ (2:20; Rom. 6:2–6). That is why he no longer sets his mind on earthly things as his treasure: the man who lived for them is dead. His old identity is not merely improved or restrained; it is in the grave with Christ. A new self has been raised in its place.

“Your life is hidden with Christ in God.” Your true life — the real you, your new resurrection life in Christ — “is hidden” (a settled, permanent state), and the word carries two glorious senses at once. First, hidden means safe: your life is stored away, locked up, in the most secure place in all the universe — with Christ, who is himself in God. It is double-wrapped: your life in Christ, and Christ in God. No enemy, no power, no sin, no devil, not death itself can reach in and snatch it (John 10:28–29). Second, hidden means concealed: your true life and glory are not on display yet. The world cannot see it, and even you do not yet see it in full — for now it looks ordinary, unremarkable, often weak. But hidden is not lost; it is stored, waiting for the day it will be unveiled (v. 4).

This sounds lofty — but here is why Old Joe can rejoice. It may read like high mysticism, yet it is the most down-to-earth comfort a struggling believer could have. First, he is utterly secure. Old Joe’s real life — his salvation, his standing with God, his future, his very self — is not held in his own trembling hands; it is locked away with Christ in God, in the safest vault in existence. He cannot lose it. On his worst day, when he feels a failure and a fraud, his life is still safe, because it does not hang on his performance or his feelings but is hidden with Christ in God. Second, he is not yet what he will be. Right now Old Joe may look like nothing much — ordinary, aging, weary, unimpressive; the world sees no glory in him, and he may feel none. That is because his real life is hidden for now, like a seed buried in winter ground, like an acorn that does not yet look like the oak. But the glory is real, and it is coming: when Christ appears, what is hidden will burst into the open (v. 4). So Old Joe can lift his head. He does not have to achieve his life, guard it, or prove it; it is kept safe with Christ in God, and its hidden glory is on its way. cf. 1 John 3:2; Col. 2:3.

verseByVerse.quote: When Christ who is your life appears, then you also will appear with him in glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The new note — and how it fits. Having spoken of present realities — you have been raised (v. 1), you have died, your life is hidden (v. 3) — Paul now lifts the eyes to the future, to the day of Christ’s return. This is the capstone of the whole paragraph and the answer to its deepest “why.” Why seek the things above and set the mind there? Because your life is hidden with Christ now (v. 3), and it will not stay hidden: when he appears, it will blaze into the open in glory. The pattern is hidden-now, revealed-then. And this verse is also the hinge of the letter’s argument: having settled who the believer is and will be (vv. 1–4), Paul is about to draw the practical conclusion — “Put to death therefore…” (v. 5). The future glory is the great motive for present holiness.

“Christ who is your life”. Notice the breathtaking phrase. Paul does not say Christ merely gives us life, as though life were a gift we then hold apart from him; he says Christ is our life — its source, its substance, its very centre. To have Christ is to have life; to be without him is to be without it. He is not an addition to Old Joe’s life, one good thing among many — he is Old Joe’s life. (This is the final answer to a heresy that offered Christ-plus: Christ is not part of the package; he is the whole of it.) cf. Gal. 2:20; Phil. 1:21; John 11:25.

“When Christ…appears”. The word means to be made manifest, brought out of hiding into open view. Right now Christ is hidden — enthroned at God’s right hand, unseen by the world. But a day is fixed when he will be revealed in glory and power before the whole creation, no longer veiled. And mark the word “when,” not “if”: his appearing is certain; only the hour is unknown.

“You also will appear with him in glory”. Here the believer’s destiny is bound fast to Christ’s. As his life is now hidden with Christ, so it will be revealed with Christ: when the Lord is unveiled, his people will be unveiled alongside him — and not in shame but “in glory.” The hidden life of v. 3 will be displayed at last, and Old Joe, who looks like nothing much now, will shine with the very glory of Christ, transformed into his likeness (1 John 3:2; Phil. 3:21; Rom. 8:17–18). The ordinary believer will be revealed in radiance beside the King of the universe.

This all sounds lofty — but here is Old Joe’s joy. Strip it down and it is the surest, most thrilling future a man could have. Right now Old Joe is hidden — plain, weary, unremarkable, often struggling, with nothing the world would call glorious about him. But a day is fixed when Christ will burst into view, and on that day Old Joe will burst into view with him, sharing his glory. What he truly is will finally be seen. Think of an heir to a great throne who has lived his whole life unrecognised, in working clothes, and the day of the coronation comes: he is led out, robed, and revealed before all as the king’s own son. That is Old Joe. He does not have to earn this glory, or guard it, or prove it — it is fixed and certain, because it is tied to Christ’s own appearing, which cannot fail. His story does not end in the grave or in obscurity; it ends in glory, with Christ. So he can carry the dullness and weakness of now with his head up: the best is not behind him and not even merely ahead of him — it is coming, and it is sure. cf. 1 John 3:2–3.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–11 — Put to Death, Put Off
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The imperative flows straight from the indicative: because you have died with Christ (v. 3), put to death what is earthly in you (v. 5). The word is violent — kill, execute — for sin is an enemy to be slain, not a pet to be tamed; yet this is no return to chapter 2’s flesh-punishing rules, which cannot touch the heart. It is mortification by the Spirit, from a standing already secured: become what you already are. The first list of sins runs from the outward deed inward to the desire — immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire — climaxing in covetousness, which Paul flatly names idolatry, the craving that sets created things where God alone belongs. Such sins are no trifles: the wrath of God is coming against them, and they were the very air the Colossians once breathed — though that life is now decisively past.

So Paul turns to a second image: “put them all away,” strip them off like filthy clothes — the anger that smoulders, the wrath that flares, the malice beneath both, the slander and the obscene talk that empty a corrupt heart through the mouth. And the deep ground of it all is stated twice: “you have put off the old self” and “have put on the new self.” The change of clothing has already happened, once for all, in Christ; the daily putting-off and putting-on simply live out an accomplished reality. Meanwhile that new self “is being renewed” — an ongoing work of God — “in knowledge after the image of its creator”: sanctification is nothing less than the restoration of the defaced image of God, the patient cleaning of a painted-over portrait until the likeness of Christ shines out again.

And this new self is corporate as well as personal. In it the great walls of the old humanity — race, religion, culture, class, down to the most despised Scythian — no longer divide; they are not erased as facts but dethroned. “Christ is all, and in all”: the one thing that finally defines a person is whether Christ is his, and the same indwelling Christ in every believer is what makes them one.
verseByVerse.theology:
Mortification: Putting to Death What Christ Has Already Condemned

John Owen’s great treatise On the Mortification of Sin is the most sustained Reformed treatment of what Paul commands in Colossians 3:5. Owen’s central principle — “be killing sin, or it will be killing you” — reflects Paul’s logic exactly. The mortification Paul calls for is not the ascetic self-punishment that the Colossian false teachers practiced and Paul has just condemned (2:23); it is the Spirit-enabled application of the cross to specific sinful desires, the practical reckoning with what Christ accomplished: these desires belong to the old self that died in Christ; by the Spirit I put them to death.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossians were being offered an ascetic program that promised to deal with the flesh by external denial. Paul says: that program has no value in stopping the flesh’s indulgence (2:23). The real program is mortification — not external prohibition but the internal death-dealing of the Spirit to specific desires. The difference is not severity (asceticism can be more severe than mortification) but source: mortification flows from union with the crucified Christ. Now: The Christian who is fighting sin through willpower and self-discipline alone is using the wrong weapons. Mortification is spiritual warfare: the application of Christ’s death to specific sin patterns, in prayer, by the Spirit, in the community of faith. The fight is real; the weapon is the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: Put to death therefore what is earthly in you: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Put to death therefore” — the flow of the argument. The “therefore” reaches back to vv. 1–4. Because you have died and been raised with Christ, because your life is hidden with him and will appear with him in glory — therefore put the old sins to death. This is the great pattern of the Christian life: become what you are. You died to the old life as a finished fact (v. 3); now daily put to death its lingering expressions. And note the sharp contrast with chapter 2: this is not the asceticism Paul just condemned — rules and severity imposed from outside, which cannot touch the flesh (2:23) — but the killing of sin from the inside, by those already dead-and-raised with Christ.

“Put to death” — what, and how, for Old Joe. The word (nekroō) is violent: kill, execute, put to death. Not manage, not tame, not go easy on — kill. Sin is to be treated as an enemy to be executed, not a pet to be domesticated. What is to be killed? “What is earthly in you” — the sinful desires and habits of the old earthly nature that still cling to the believer (Paul lists them next). How? Here is the handle Old Joe needs. It is a paradox with v. 3: he has died with Christ once for all, yet he must put sin to death daily — the finished fact is exactly what fuels the ongoing fight. The killing is not done by the flesh-punishing rules of chapter 2; it is done “by the Spirit” (Rom. 8:13), in the strength of God, and from the standing of a man who already belongs to Christ. In practice that means Old Joe names the sin as the enemy it is, refuses it, starves it, flees the temptation, says a decisive and ruthless no — and does it leaning the whole way on the Spirit’s power, not gritting his teeth to earn God’s favour but fighting from a favour already his. “Be killing sin, or it will be killing you.”

“What is earthly in you”. Literally, “the members that are upon the earth” — the impulses and practices that belong to the earthly, fallen self. The link back to v. 2 is deliberate: these are the very “things on earth” the mind is not to be set on, now to be put to death. And note “in you” — the battlefield is inside, in the believer’s own remaining corruption. Then Paul names five, and the order is telling: he digs from the outward act down to the inward root.

The five named — from the deed to the desire. Sexual immorality (porneia) is the broad word for every sexual act outside marriage — fornication, adultery, prostitution, the lot (it gives us “pornography”); the outward deed. Impurity (akatharsia) moves inward — moral uncleanness, the defiled imagination and polluted inner life, not only the act but the filth behind it. Passion (pathos) goes deeper still — the ungoverned, driving lust that masters a person. Evil desire (epithymia kakē) reaches the very bottom — the wrong craving of the heart itself, the wanting that is set on what God forbids. Paul is exposing something vital here: sin is not merely bad behaviour to be tidied up on the surface; it runs all the way down into what the heart wants. That is why rules alone (chapter 2) can never cure it — they trim the deed and leave the desire alive.

“And covetousness, which is idolatry”. Paul crowns the list with a startling identification. Covetousness (pleonexia) is greed — the restless craving for more, the grasping after possessions, money, things that are not yours. And Paul calls it flatly what it is: idolatry. Why? Because to covet is to set the heart’s supreme desire and trust on something other than God — to look to created things for the security, satisfaction, and worth that God alone can give. Whatever a man treasures and trusts above God is his functional god; the greedy man bows at the altar of his own wallet (cf. Eph. 5:5; Matt. 6:24). This is why covetousness climaxes the list: it lays bare the idolatry beneath all these sins — every one of them is, at root, seeking in something other than God the life that only God can give. And it is the sneakiest of sins, for it wears a respectable coat: just “wanting a bit more,” just “a nicer life.” The cure is the same as the whole chapter’s: when Christ himself is your life (v. 4), the idols lose their grip. cf. Luke 12:15; Heb. 13:5.

verseByVerse.quote: On account of these the wrath of God is coming.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The flow of the argument. Between the two lists of sins (v. 5 and v. 8) Paul pauses to give the reason they must be killed and stripped off: “On account of these the wrath of God is coming.” Why deal so ruthlessly with these sins? Because they are exactly what God’s judgment is set against. The wrath of God is the dark backdrop that makes putting sin to death not optional but urgent.

“The wrath of God is coming” — what does this mean? First, what God’s wrath is not: it is not a bad temper, a petty loss of control, or God flying off the handle. The wrath of God is the settled, holy, righteous opposition of a perfectly good God to all evil — his just and judicial reaction against sin. Far from a flaw, it is the necessary mark of his goodness: a judge who felt no opposition to injustice would be no good judge, and a God indifferent to evil would be no good God. Second, “is coming”: this wrath is real and on its way; a day of judgment is fixed (Rom. 2:5). These sins, then, are no trifles to be excused or kept as pets — they are the very things divine judgment is advancing against. For the believer there is deep sobriety here, and also deep relief: this is the very wrath that fell on Christ in his place (2:14), so that we are rescued from the wrath to come (1 Thess. 1:10) — which is all the more reason not to go back and dabble in what cost the Saviour so much. cf. Eph. 5:6; Rom. 1:18.

verseByVerse.quote: In these you too once walked, when you were living in them.
verseByVerse.commentary: “In these you too once walked” — is Paul saying every unbeliever does all these things? No — and the distinction matters. Paul is not claiming that every person outside Christ commits every sin on the list, or that all are equally vile in their conduct. People apart from Christ differ enormously; many are outwardly decent, kind, and restrained, for God’s common grace holds back the full flood of sin in the world. What Paul is saying is two things. First, this was the Colossians’ own former life: they “once walked” (it was their habitual road) in these very sins, “when you were living in them” (when such things were the element they lived and breathed in). Second, and more deeply, these sins are the native air of life apart from God — the realm the old life belongs to, its natural tendency and fruit, whether or not every sin shows its face in every person. The unredeemed heart is turned from God at the root (1:21), and this is the direction that turning runs. Notice the tender words “you too”: even you, now God’s holy people, were once in this. That is meant to do two things — to keep the believer humble (do not look down on those still trapped; you were there yourself) and to make him grateful (grace reached in and lifted you out). And it sets up the great pivot of v. 8: once you walked there — but now. That was your old country; you have emigrated; do not move back. cf. 1 Cor. 6:11; Titus 3:3–5.

verseByVerse.quote: But now you must put them all away: anger, wrath, malice, slander, and obscene talk from your mouth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“But now you must put them all away” — is this the same as “put to death,” and how is it done? “But now” is the great hinge from the old life to the new. The command “put away” shifts the picture: where v. 5 said kill (sin as an enemy to be executed), v. 8 says take off — like stripping off filthy, stinking clothes and throwing them aside. It is the same fundamental call to deal decisively with sin, under a new image: kill the root, strip off the garment. But how — for Old Joe, who has tried so often to “just stop” and still struggles? Here is the help. First, this is not mere willpower and white-knuckle suppression in his own strength; that is the chapter-2 asceticism that cannot conquer the flesh. Second, putting off always comes paired with putting on (v. 10, v. 12): you do not overcome a sin by leaving a hole where it was, but by replacing it — take off anger and put on compassion, take off lying and become a teller of truth. Sin is expelled not by a vacuum but by a stronger affection. Third, it flows from who he already is: he strips off these sins “seeing that he has already put off the old self” (v. 9) — he is not fighting to become someone new, but living out the new man he already is. And fourth, it is the work of a lifetime, done by the Spirit (Rom. 8:13) and carried along by God’s own renewing (v. 10). So Old Joe’s ongoing struggle is not proof that he has failed or that he is not truly Christ’s; it is the normal shape of the Christian fight. The old clothes feel familiar, and he keeps reaching for them — so he keeps taking them off again, day after day, leaning on the Spirit, and God keeps remaking him. Progress, not yet perfection. cf. Eph. 4:22–24; Heb. 12:1.

Anger, wrath, malice — the sins of the heart. Paul names three that lie close together but differ. Anger (orgē) is the settled, smouldering kind — the slow-burning resentment, the grudge nursed and harboured, the banked fire of ill-feeling that will not go out. Wrath (thymos) is the sudden kind — the flare-up, the outburst, the boiling-over of temper that explodes and (often) subsides: the blaze rather than the embers. Malice is the root beneath both — the ill-will itself, the meanness of spirit that actually wishes another harm. Paul reaches past the hot words to the cold intent: the desire to see someone hurt. All three must come off.

Slander — and when is it slander, and when is it a fair warning? Slander (blasphēmia) is injurious speech against others — running a person down, tearing at his reputation, speaking evil of him. But Old Joe rightly asks: how do I tell slander from a legitimate warning? Scripture itself names real dangers and even real names (Paul warns of Hymenaeus, of Demas), so speaking of another’s fault is not always sin. The difference lies in three tests. Is it true? Slander traffics in falsehood, distortion, and the exaggeration that makes a tale juicier; a fair warning is accurate. Is it necessary, and for a good end? A warning aims to protect someone from real harm, or to help the person himself; slander serves only to wound, to entertain, or to make the speaker look better by comparison. And why am I really saying it — in love or in malice? A faithful warning is given reluctantly, in love, and usually to the person who can actually do something about it; slander is told with relish, behind the back, to anyone who will listen. So before Old Joe speaks of another’s fault, three questions: Is it true? Is it kind and necessary? And why am I saying it? If it is true, spoken in love, and needed to protect, that is warning. If it runs a man down for the pleasure of it, or to lift myself above him, that is slander.

Obscene talk — the sin of the mouth. Last comes “obscene talk from your mouth” — foul, filthy, shameful speech: dirty language, coarse obscenity, the abusive and degrading word. Notice how Paul’s list has travelled — from the hidden heart (anger, wrath, malice) out to the open mouth (slander, obscene talk): the corruption within finally spills out in what we say. The tongue is the drain through which the heart empties (Matt. 12:34), which is why the new self must guard the mouth.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not lie to one another, seeing that you have put off the old self with its practices and have put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Do not lie to one another”. One more sin of speech, given its own command: lying — and not only bald untruths but half-truths, spin, flattery, broken promises, the whole family of deceit. “To one another” presses it home: lying poisons the trust that holds the new community together, and so it is an assault on the very unity Paul is about to celebrate (v. 11). The new people of God are a people of truth, for their God is the God of truth and the devil is the father of lies (John 8:44); to deceive is to wear the old father’s likeness, not the new.

“You have put off the old self” — already done, or still to be done? And what is the “old self”? The verb is a completed past act: you have put it off — already, decisively, done. The “old self” (literally the “old man”) is not merely a bundle of bad habits; it is the whole person you used to be in Adam — your old identity and nature under the reign of sin, “with its practices,” the entire way of life that went with it. And Scripture says that old self was stripped off and crucified with Christ at your conversion (Rom. 6:6). So the foundational answer is: already done. The old man is not being slowly removed a piece at a time; he was taken off once for all in Christ. What remains — the daily putting-away of his leftover practices (vv. 5, 8) — is not the removal of the old self but the living-out of a removal already accomplished. That is the whole logic here: because the old self is already off, keep stripping off its rags.

“And have put on the new self” — already done, or still to be done? And what is it? Again a completed act: you have put on the new self. The “new self” (the “new man”) is the new person you now are in Christ — the regenerate self, the new creation (2 Cor. 5:17), your new identity in union with the risen Lord. It is also corporate: the new humanity Christ is forming, which is why v. 11 immediately says that in this new self the old divisions of race and class fall away. So both the putting-off and the putting-on are stated as done: in Christ, Old Joe has already taken off the old man and put on the new. His identity is settled. And yet — as the next words show — that new self, already put on, is not static.

“Which is being renewed” — the ongoing work. Here the tense changes: from the finished “put off / put on” to the continuous “is being renewed.” The new self, once and for all put on, is now in a process of constant renewal — made new, day by day. And it is passive: God is the one renewing it (cf. 2 Cor. 4:16; Rom. 12:2). So here is the answer to the puzzle of “already, or not yet?” — it is both. The decisive change is done (the old off, the new on: that is your settled identity); the transformation is ongoing (the new self being renewed: that is your daily growth). This is sanctification, and God himself is at work in it.

“In knowledge” — what is meant? The new self is being renewed “in knowledge” — and this is no dry collecting of facts, and certainly not the counterfeit secret “knowledge” the false teachers peddled. It is the true, deep, personal knowledge of God (epignōsis): coming to know him as he really is, in Christ, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden (2:3). The fall plunged the human mind into ignorance and darkness about God (Rom. 1:21; Eph. 4:18); the renewal reverses it — we come to know God truly again, and as we know him, we are remade. Knowing God rightly is itself transforming: you become like what you most truly know and behold.

“After the image of its creator”. The renewal is shaping the new self according to “the image of its creator” — and this reaches all the way back to the beginning. Man was made “in the image of God” (Gen. 1:26–27), and that image was defaced — though not erased — by the fall. Now, in Christ, God is restoring it: remaking the new self after the very image in which it was first created. And remember who the perfect image is — Christ himself, “the image of the invisible God” (1:15). So to be renewed after the image of the Creator is to be conformed to Christ (Rom. 8:29; 2 Cor. 3:18). Sanctification is nothing less than this: God re-stamping his own likeness on the human soul, restoring in you the image that was ruined in Eden.

So that Old Joe gets it — and takes heart. Put the whole picture together. Coming to Christ was like stripping off filthy, ragged old work clothes — the old self with all its sins — and putting on a clean new set — the new self in Christ. That change of clothes has already happened, once and for all: Old Joe is dressed in the new man. So the daily Christian life is simply this — live as the man you now are: keep taking off the scraps of the old filthy clothing you still find yourself reaching for (the sins of vv. 5 and 8), and keep wearing the new. And here is the heart of it for a struggler: while he does, God is at work on him like a master restorer cleaning a great portrait that has been painted over and grimed with age — patiently bringing back, stroke by stroke, the original image of the King that the fall had buried. Old Joe cannot always see the progress, and the cleaning can be slow; but the Master does not abandon a portrait he has begun to restore (Phil. 1:6). So when Old Joe still struggles, the answer is not despair but this twofold truth: the decisive change is done (you are the new man, clothed in Christ), and the renewal is under way (God is restoring his image in you). Keep putting off, keep putting on, and leave the renewing to the Restorer. cf. 2 Cor. 3:18; Rom. 8:29.

verseByVerse.quote: Here there is not Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave, free; but Christ is all, and in all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This looks like a new topic — but it is not. Paul has been speaking of putting off the old self and putting on the new (vv. 9–10); now he says that in this new self the old human divisions disappear. The link is the “new man.” The new self is not only personal but corporate — Christ is forming a whole new humanity, a new people — and in that new people the walls that divide the old humanity no longer stand. The renewal of God’s image in the individual (v. 10) goes hand in hand with the creation of one new people out of every kind of person.

“Not Greek and Jew…barbarian, Scythian, slave, free” — why list these? Paul names the great dividing-lines of his world, across every category. Greek and Jew — race and ethnicity, the deepest divide of all. Circumcised and uncircumcised — religion, the badge that marked the two apart. Barbarian, Scythian — culture: a “barbarian” was anyone whose speech sounded like babble to Greek ears, the uncivilized; and the Scythian was the byword for the lowest, wildest, most savage of all — Paul deliberately reaches to the most despised example imaginable. Slave, free — social class, the great fault-line of the Roman world. Race, religion, culture, class: Paul sweeps up the whole spectrum of human division, down to the most extreme, to make one point — in the new humanity, none of these any longer defines a person or divides the body. There is no one so foreign, so low, so looked-down-upon that he cannot be one in Christ with anyone else. The walls that structured the entire ancient world (and ours) come down at the foot of the cross. They are not erased as facts — a Jew is still a Jew, a slave still a slave — but they are dethroned: they no longer decide a person’s worth, his standing before God, or his place in the family.

“But Christ is all, and in all” — what Old Joe must grasp. Here is the glorious replacement for all those labels. “Christ is all” — he is everything, the sum and substance, the one thing that finally counts. In place of the old categories that ranked and divided people, there is now a single defining reality: Christ. And “in all” — the same Christ lives in every one of his people, Jew or Greek, slave or free, polished or rough. That indwelling is what makes them one. Three things for Old Joe to take home. First, his worth and identity are no longer measured by the things the world ranks people by — his nationality, his job, his class, his schooling, whether he is “somebody” or “nobody” in the world’s eyes. Christ is all; the only thing that ultimately defines him is that he belongs to Christ and Christ is in him. Second, this makes him truly one with every other believer, however different — richer or poorer, of another race or background; they share the one indwelling Christ, so they are family, and Old Joe must never let the world’s divisions divide the church. Third, here is the wonder: the same Christ in whom all the fullness of God dwells (1:19) lives in plain, ordinary Old Joe. He is not on the outside of the blessing looking in — Christ is in him. cf. Gal. 3:28; Eph. 2:14–16.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
If the old self is stripped off, the new self must be clothed: “put on.” And Paul roots the command in identity before he names a single virtue — “as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved.” These graces are not a program to earn God’s favour but the wardrobe that suits those who already have it; the beloved can afford to love. So the new self puts on compassion and kindness, true humility (not the self-hating or showy counterfeit of chapter 2) and meekness (strength under control, not weakness), and patience — worked out in the friction of real church life as bearing with one another’s faults and forgiving real wrongs. And the measure of forgiveness is staggering: “as the Lord has forgiven you” — freely, fully, before we ever asked. Over all these is drawn the one garment that holds the rest together: love, the bond of perfect harmony.

From character Paul moves to the community’s shared life, and three things govern it. The peace of Christ is to umpire the heart and the body, making the call when tensions pull the one body apart. The word of Christ is to dwell richly — a resident, not a guest — overflowing into the mutual ministry of teaching and admonishing one another in wisdom, and into psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs that lodge the truth in the heart. And the whole is summed up in the most sweeping statement of Christ’s lordship in the New Testament: “whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus.” There is no secular corner; the humblest task, done as Christ’s representative and for his honour, becomes worship. And threaded through the entire section — three times in three verses — runs its keynote: thankfulness. The community that puts on the new self is a peace-ruled, Word-saturated, singing, and above all thankful people.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Virtues of the New Self as the Character of Christ

The list of virtues in Colossians 3:12–15 is nothing less than a portrait of Christ himself: compassionate, kind, humble, meek, patient, forgiving, loving, peaceful. Reformed theology understands sanctification as progressive conformity to the image of Christ (Rom 8:29); the virtues Paul commands here are the specific contours of that image. They are not generated by the believer through moral effort; they are produced by the Spirit as the fruit of genuine union with Christ (compare the fruit of the Spirit in Galatians 5:22–23). The community that puts on these virtues is the community that is becoming what it already is in Christ: holy and beloved.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossian community, like every early Christian community, was a mixture of people from very different backgrounds — Jewish, Greek, slave, free — with very different habits of relating and conflicting. The virtues Paul commands were counter-cultural in every direction: humility was scorned by Graeco-Roman aristocratic culture; forgiveness was a novelty in a world organized around honour and revenge. Now: The church remains the most diverse social reality in the world, and the virtues Paul commands remain equally counter-cultural. The church that is genuinely putting on compassion, kindness, humility, and forbearance will look radically different from any other community the world contains, because these virtues are the character of the one who was raised for us.

verseByVerse.quote: Put on then, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassionate hearts, kindness, humility, meekness, and patience, bearing with one another and, if one has a complaint against another, forgiving each other; as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive. And above all these put on love, which binds everything together in perfect harmony.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Put on” — and how? The clothing image continues. Having stripped off the old sins (vv. 8–9), the believer now puts on the new virtues — he gets dressed in the character of Christ. The Christian life is never merely stopping the bad; it is actively clothing yourself with the good. How is it done? Deliberately and daily, the way you put on clothes each morning — you choose to act in compassion, kindness, patience, even before the feeling arrives, and very often the feeling follows the action. It is done from your identity (the next words, “as God’s chosen ones”), as the new person you already are. And it is done by the Spirit, for these graces are the fruit he bears (Gal. 5:22–23) and the very likeness of Christ — to put them on is to “put on Christ” (Rom. 13:14). This is the opposite of chapter 2’s rule-keeping: not severity imposed from outside, but Christ’s own character grown from within.

“As God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved” — why does Paul start here? Before he names a single virtue, Paul names who they are — three words, and all three are God’s prior work on them. Chosen (the elect): God set his love on them and picked them out before they had done anything to deserve it (Eph. 1:4) — the very title once given to Israel, now worn by all who are in Christ. Holy: set apart as God’s own treasured people. Beloved: dearly loved by God, sharing the belovedness of his beloved Son (1:13). This is no accident of order. The identity comes before the commands, and the commands flow from it. Old Joe does not put on these graces in order to become chosen, holy, and loved; he puts them on because he already is. And that changes everything: a man secure in being chosen and loved can afford to pour himself out for others — he loves from a fullness, not to earn one. The beloved can afford to love.

“Compassionate hearts, kindness”. The first garments are tender ones. Compassionate hearts — literally a “heart of mercy,” a gut-level pity that is genuinely moved by another’s pain and stirred to help; not cold duty but felt tenderness, the inward parts wrung by someone’s need. Kindness is that compassion turned into action — the gracious, generous disposition that actually does good to others, treats them gently, goes out of its way to help. Compassion feels; kindness acts. It is the very kindness of God himself, which leads us to repentance (Rom. 2:4).

“Humility” — and let us be clear what it is and is not. Strikingly, this is the very word the false teachers had twisted into ascetic show (2:18, 23); here is the real thing. True humility is a right estimate of yourself before God — knowing you are a sinner saved by sheer grace, wholly dependent on him, and therefore not above anyone; it “counts others more significant than yourself” (Phil. 2:3) and stoops to serve, as Christ himself stooped (Phil. 2:5–8). But note what humility is not. It is not thinking you are worthless, or wallowing in self-hatred — that is just self-absorption with a long face. It is not the fishing-for-compliments false modesty of the heretics. And it is not spinelessness or being a doormat. Humility is not thinking less of yourself; it is thinking of yourself less — the self forgotten because the eyes are on God and on others.

“Meekness and patience”. Meekness, too, is widely misunderstood, so hear what it is and is not. It is not weakness, timidity, or spinelessness — not the man who cannot stand up for anything. The Greeks used the word for a wild horse that had been broken and tamed: all its power still there, but now under control, harnessed, gentle to the hand. So meekness is strength under control — the gentleness of one who could retaliate but chooses not to, who does not insist on his rights or lash back. Jesus was “gentle and lowly” (Matt. 11:29) yet cleansed the temple; Moses was “very meek” yet led a nation. Patience is literally being “long-tempered” — the opposite of short-tempered: slow to anger, able to endure provocation and difficult people without exploding or giving up. It is God’s own patience with us (Rom. 2:4) worn toward others.

“Bearing with one another”. Here the virtues meet real life in the church. To “bear with” is to put up with one another — to endure each other’s rough edges, quirks, and irritating ways without letting them rupture the fellowship. Old Joe knows the cases: the brother who talks far too long, the one whose opinions grate, the sister always late, the personality that rubs him entirely the wrong way. To bear with them is to make allowance, to overlook the irritation, to keep loving them as they are rather than freezing them out — the way a family puts up with one another’s annoying habits around the same breakfast table, because they are family. Every church needs this daily, for people are wearing, and love bears with them.

“Forgiving each other…as the Lord has forgiven you” — and must I wait until they ask? Bearing-with handles the small irritations; forgiveness handles the real wrongs — “if one has a complaint against another,” an actual grievance. Suppose a fellow believer truly wrongs Old Joe: gossips about him, cheats him, lets him down badly, wounds him with a cutting word. To forgive is to release the debt — to refuse the grudge and the revenge, and not let the injury harden into a wall — just as God cancelled Old Joe’s own vast debt (2:14). And the measure is staggering: “as the Lord has forgiven you” — freely, fully, at infinite cost, and before you ever asked, while you were still his enemy (Rom. 5:8–10). So must Old Joe forgive only when the other apologizes, or just like that? Both halves of the answer matter. The forgiving heart — the release of bitterness, the refusal of revenge, the readiness and longing to forgive — he must have always, at once, whether or not the other ever asks; that is how the Lord forgave him, taking the first step while he was still in the wrong (Mark 11:25; Luke 23:34). He is never to nurse a grudge until the offender grovels. The full reconciliation — the “I forgive you” spoken and received, the relationship restored — is completed when the other turns and repents (Luke 17:3); restoration, by its nature, takes two. So Old Joe forgives from the heart immediately, holding nothing back, and stands ready, even eager, to fold the other back into full fellowship the moment he turns.

“And above all these put on love, which binds everything together in perfect harmony”. Love is the crowning garment — “above all these,” the outer robe pulled on over the whole wardrobe of virtues. What is this love? Not mainly a warm feeling, not romance, not merely liking someone — you can love, that is, seek the good of, a person you do not naturally like. It is a settled commitment of the will to seek another’s good and to give yourself for it, at cost, regardless of merit or return — the love that “so loved…that he gave,” the love mapped out in 1 Corinthians 13. So it is not soft sentiment and not mere permissiveness; it is self-giving action. And why “above all”? Because love is the bond — syndesmos, a ligament (the very picture of 2:19) — that ties all the other graces together and ties the whole body of believers together “in perfect harmony,” in mature completeness. Compassion, kindness, humility, meekness, patience: without love they fall apart and ring hollow (1 Cor. 13:1–3); with love drawn over them all, they are bound into one beautiful, whole, mature character. Love is the thread that holds the entire garment together. cf. Rom. 13:8–10; John 13:34–35.

verseByVerse.quote: And let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, to which indeed you were called in one body. And be thankful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts” — what, and how? The “peace of Christ” is the peace he won and gives — the peace he made “by the blood of his cross” (1:20): first, peace with God, the war ended and the sinner reconciled; and out of that, the settled, untroubled calm he leaves with his people (“my peace I give to you,” John 14:27), and the peace that should reign between them. And the word “rule” (brabeuetō) is the umpire’s word — the referee who makes the call and settles the contest. So Paul says: let Christ’s peace be the umpire in your heart. When you are torn or anxious, when relationships are strained, when a decision pulls you two ways, let his peace make the call — refuse what shatters it, choose what preserves it. Do not let anger, fear, or self-will referee your heart; let the peace of Christ do it.

“To which indeed you were called in one body”. Two things. First, this peace is part of your calling — God did not call you to strife but to peace (1 Cor. 7:15); it is not optional but the very thing you were summoned to. Second, you were called “in one body” — into the one body of Christ, the church (recall v. 11, the one new humanity made of every kind of person). So this peace is not merely a private inner calm; it is the bond meant to govern the body’s life together. Old Joe is no lone Christian; he was called into a body, and the same peace that should umpire his heart is to keep the whole church one.

“And be thankful”. A short command, but no afterthought — it is the first of three calls to thanksgiving in three verses (vv. 15, 16, 17), for gratitude is the keynote of this whole section. And it belongs right here, beside peace, because the thankful heart is the peaceful heart. Gratitude crowds out the grumbling, discontent, and sense of grievance that breed strife and anxiety; the man counting his mercies has no room to nurse complaints (cf. Phil. 4:6–7). A thankful Christian is a contented, peaceable Christian, and a thankful church is a peaceful one.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, teaching and admonishing one another in all wisdom, singing psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, with thankfulness in your hearts to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“The word of Christ” — what is it? The phrase is unique to this verse. It means the message that is Christ’s — the gospel of which he is the heart, the apostolic teaching about him and from him that the Colossians received (“the word of the truth, the gospel,” 1:5). It is not narrowly only the red-letter sayings of Jesus, but the whole word that proclaims him; and rightly applied it embraces all of Scripture, which everywhere testifies to Christ and comes from him. Note the pointed contrast: let Christ’s word fill you — not the “philosophy and empty deceit” and human traditions of the false teachers (2:8, 22).

“Dwell in you richly” — what and how? “Dwell” means to take up residence — to live in, to settle, to make a home — not to drop by as an occasional visitor. And “richly” means abundantly, lavishly, in full and spacious measure. So the word of Christ is to be a resident, not a guest, and a richly-housed one — furnishing every room of the heart and of the church’s common life. How? By deep and regular intake — reading, hearing, pondering, memorizing — and by the two channels Paul names next: mutual teaching and corporate singing. This is, in fact, how all the putting-off and putting-on of the previous verses actually happens: the mind is renewed (v. 10) as the Word takes up rich residence within. Let it so fill the house that it shapes everything.

“Teaching and admonishing one another in all wisdom”. The richly-dwelling Word overflows into a mutual ministry. Teaching is the positive imparting of truth — helping one another understand and grow. Admonishing is the corrective side — warning, counseling, urging a brother away from wrong and toward right (the same word Paul used of his own ministry, 1:28). And mark “one another”: this is not the task of the official teachers alone but of every member — ordinary believers ministering the Word to each other. It is to be done “in all wisdom” — skillfully and fittingly, with discernment to know what word the moment needs and how to speak it. So Old Joe both receives this and gives it; the Word in him is meant to overflow to others.

“Singing psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, with thankfulness”. The third overflow of the indwelling Word is song. Paul names a rich variety — psalms (the inspired Old Testament songbook), hymns (songs of praise to God and Christ, perhaps like the great hymn of 1:15–20), and spiritual songs (Spirit-prompted song of every kind); we need not press rigid distinctions, for together they mean the full range of sung worship. And notice: singing is itself a way the Word “dwells richly” and a form of “teaching one another” (so the parallel in Eph. 5:19) — sung truth lodges in the heart and ministers to the whole congregation as nothing else does. It is to be done “with thankfulness in your hearts to God” — gratitude again, now lifted in praise. Worship is the Word set to music in a thankful heart.

verseByVerse.quote: And whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Whatever you do, in word or deed”. This is the sweeping summary of the whole section, and one of the most comprehensive statements of Christ’s lordship in all of Scripture. “Whatever” — nothing is left out. “In word or deed” — everything you say and everything you do, the two halves that together cover the whole of life. Not merely the “religious” parts, but the entire ordinary round — work, family, meals, rest, the chat in the street. There is no secular corner walled off from Christ; the whole of Old Joe’s Monday belongs under this word.

“Do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus”. To act “in someone’s name” is to act as his representative — on his behalf, under his authority, for his honour, in dependence on him, and in a way worthy of him. So to do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus is to live as his man in all things: to drive the van, pay the bill, speak the word, and do the task as Christ’s representative, for his glory, by his help, in a manner that would not shame his name. This both consecrates the ordinary (the humblest task becomes service of Christ) and constrains the sinful (you cannot do in his name what dishonours it). Here is the heart of the whole ethical section — not a fence of external rules, as the false teachers wanted (2:20–23), but the lordship of Christ reaching into every word and deed from the inside.

“Giving thanks to God the Father through him”. And the third call to thanksgiving in three verses closes the section: everything done in Jesus’ name is to be wrapped in gratitude to the Father. “Through him” — our thanks, like all our approach to God, comes to the Father through Christ, the one Mediator through whom our worship is welcome (the final quiet answer to the angel-mediators of chapter 2: no other channel is needed or allowed). So the new life in its daily round has two marks woven through all of it: it is lived in the name of the Lord Jesus, and it overflows in thanks to the Father through him. Lordship and gratitude — every word and deed turned into worship. cf. 1 Cor. 10:31; Eph. 5:20.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
With the great doctrine of the new self in place (3:1–17), Paul brings the lordship of Christ home — quite literally — to the household, the ordinary roof under which most of life was lived. He does not tear down the structures of the ancient home; he fills them with a wholly new spirit. The drumbeat of the whole passage is one phrase repeated in varied form — “as is fitting in the Lord,” “fearing the Lord,” “as for the Lord and not for men,” “you also have a Master in heaven.” The risen Christ of chapter 1 is now the governing reality of the breakfast table, the nursery, and the workplace.

And Paul takes the relationships two by two, and — here is the quiet revolution — he addresses not only the subordinate but the one who holds the power, laying a costly command on the strong. Wives are to submit as is fitting in the Lord; husbands are given the harder word — to love sacrificially as Christ loved the church, and never to grow harsh or bitter. Children are to obey, a thing that pleases the Lord and bears the family likeness of the obedient Son who was himself subject at Nazareth; fathers are not to provoke and crush their children but to nurture them. Bondservants are to work heartily, with sincerity of heart, as for the Lord Christ himself — the lowliest labour rendered to the King of kings, and rewarded with an inheritance that no earthly slave could ever receive; and masters, who in that world owed their slaves nothing, are commanded to deal with them justly and fairly. In a culture where the authority of husband, father, and master was absolute, every one of these paired commands to love, nurture, and do justice was startlingly counter-cultural.

None of this is bare rule-keeping. It is the overflow of the gospel just announced: those who have died and been raised with Christ (3:1–3), who do everything “in the name of the Lord Jesus” (3:17), now let that new life reshape the most intimate relationships they have. And running underneath is a great leveller: the Lord “shows no partiality” (3:25), and even the master “has a Master in heaven” (4:1). At the foot of the cross the husband and wife, parent and child, slave and master kneel side by side as sinners saved by one grace, servants of one Lord. Paul does not, in a sentence, abolish the social order of the Roman world — but he plants within it a seed of love and equality-before-God that, properly cultivated, could never leave that order unchanged.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lordship of Christ in the Household: Sacred and Ordinary

The household code illustrates one of Reformed theology’s most important convictions: there is no sacred-secular divide. The lordship of Christ claimed in the great hymn of chapter 1 arrives in chapter 3 at the level of household management, parenting, and the workplace. Abraham Kuyper’s “every square inch” is not abstract theology; it is the practical implication of “whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus” (3:17). The Christian who is an excellent spouse, a patient parent, and an honest worker is doing theology in the most concrete possible form.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Graeco-Roman household was organized around the absolute authority of the paterfamilias — husband, father, master. His authority was legally absolute. Paul does not abolish this structure but fills it with a different spirit: love, not domination; encouragement, not provocation; justice, not exploitation. The counterpart to every command of submission is a command of love and care that was genuinely counter-cultural. Now: The application of these principles in contemporary household and work relationships continues to produce the same counter-cultural witness: the Christian employee who works with integrity “as to the Lord” even when unsupervised; the Christian employer who treats workers with justice and fairness; the Christian parent who encourages rather than exasperates. Each is a small enactment of the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: Wives, submit to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Wives, submit to your husbands” — what does it mean? First, the setting: with v. 17 Paul has said that everything is to be done in the name of the Lord Jesus, and now he brings that lordship right into the home.
