The word “submit” (hypotassō) means to order or arrange oneself under — and the form Paul uses is reflexive and voluntary: the wife places herself under, freely. It is not something the husband seizes or imposes; it is her own glad, chosen deference to her husband’s God-given role of loving leadership in the marriage (the “headship” of Eph. 5:23). Notice too that it is “to your own husbands” — this is about one marriage, not women in general deferring to men in general. Positively, it is a disposition of respect, support, and trust: a wife coming alongside her husband as his partner, honouring and strengthening his leadership rather than competing with or undermining it, and — when a real decision must finally be made and they still differ — trusting his lead. Paul even frames it as a reflection of something beautiful: the church’s glad submission to Christ (Eph. 5:24).

And, just as importantly, what it does not mean. Six things must be cleared away, for the word is so often abused. (1) It does not mean the wife is inferior. She is fully equal in worth, dignity, and standing before God — equally made in his image, equally redeemed, a co-heir of the grace of life (1 Pet. 3:7; Gal. 3:28). Submission is a matter of role and order, never of value — just as the Son is fully equal to the Father in deity yet gladly does the Father’s will. (2) It does not mean slavish obedience. Tellingly, Paul tells children and slaves to “obey” (vv. 20, 22) but tells wives to “submit” — the gentler word; a wife is not her husband’s servant or child. (3) It does not mean silence or having no voice. She is a strong helper and counterpart (Gen. 2:18); she speaks, advises, and may freely disagree — godly women in Scripture did exactly that (think of Abigail). (4) It does not mean obeying into sin. Her submission is “in the Lord,” so it can never run against the Lord; if a husband demands what God forbids, she must “obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). (5) It is not a licence for harshness or abuse — the very next verse forbids the husband to be harsh, and a wife is nowhere commanded to submit to cruelty or danger; where there is abuse, the church must protect, not preach “submit.” (6) It is not earned by the husband’s worthiness, nor is it the submission of all women to all men. In short: a strong, godly, free woman gladly honouring her own husband’s leadership — never a crushed or silenced one.

Briefly, what does it look like? Most decisions in a healthy marriage are simply made together, by agreement and mutual counsel; headship and submission rarely have to “kick in.” But picture the genuine deadlock: husband and wife have prayed, talked it through, and weighed it honestly — a move, a major purchase, a direction for the family — and they still disagree, yet a decision must be made. There the wife trusts and supports her husband’s leading rather than insisting on her own way or making him pay for it. Day to day it looks like this: she speaks well of him and to him, backs and strengthens his leadership instead of undercutting it, and treats him with genuine respect (Eph. 5:33). It is the picture of a Sarah (1 Pet. 3:5–6) — a woman of strength who freely honours her husband, not a doormat who has lost her voice.

“As is fitting in the Lord” — the argument. Paul does not ground the wife’s submission in custom, culture, or social pressure — he grounds it “in the Lord.” “Fitting” means proper, becoming, suitable; this ordering is the fitting and beautiful thing — but fitting in the Lord, that is, within the life of those who belong to Christ and live under his lordship. This is the same lordship of v. 17 (“do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus”) now reaching into the marriage. So three things follow. First, it dignifies her submission: it is not capitulation to a husband’s superiority but an act of devotion to Christ — she does it for the Lord, as part of her own walk with him, “as to the Lord” (Eph. 5:22). Second, it roots the command in Christ, not in shifting cultural fashion — it stands because he is Lord, not because society once expected it. And third, it limits the command: because her submission is “in the Lord,” it can never be a submission that dishonours the Lord. The same phrase that asks it also guards it.

verseByVerse.quote: Husbands, love your wives, and do not be harsh with them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Husbands, love your wives” — what does it mean? The word is agapē — not first of all a romantic feeling or a warm glow, but the deliberate, self-giving love of the will that seeks the wife’s good (the same love crowned in 3:14). Paul states it briefly here; his parallel letter spells out the standard in full: “Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Eph. 5:25). That is the measure — nothing less than the sacrificial, self-emptying love of Christ for his people. So the husband’s headship of v. 18 is here defined, and it turns out to be headship-by-sacrifice, not headship-by-domination: he leads by giving himself away. And mark how counter-cultural this was. The household codes of the ancient world loaded the duties onto the lesser party and told the husband almost nothing; Paul turns and lays on the man the harder command — to love his wife as Christ loved the church. It is a love that is sacrificial (her good above his own comfort), constant (a settled commitment, not rising and falling with his feelings or her loveliness on a given day), and active — it “nourishes and cherishes” her as a man cares for his own body (Eph. 5:28–29).

Briefly, what does it look like? It looks like a husband who puts his wife’s good ahead of his own comfort — giving up the evening, the hobby, the preference, to help her or simply to be with her. It looks like cherishing and nourishing her: providing, protecting, noticing, listening, speaking tenderly, building her up rather than taking her for granted. It looks like serving her in the small, daily, unglamorous ways (the Lord himself knelt to wash feet), and bearing the load with her. It looks like a man who keeps loving her on the day she is hardest to love, because his love is a covenant, not a mood. In a word, it looks like Christ — a husband who would lay himself down for his wife.

“And do not be harsh with them” — the besetting sin to avoid. The word (from pikros, “bitter”) means “do not be embittered toward them,” do not grow harsh, sharp, or sour with your wife. Having commanded love, Paul at once names love’s opposite — and he names it because it is precisely the husband’s characteristic temptation. The very strength and authority of his position can curdle into domination; a man can let small resentments harden into a cold, bitter, critical spirit toward the one he should cherish most. The present tense warns against the slow settling-in of such a spirit: do not let bitterness take root and grow.

What it looks like — and the cure. Harshness wears familiar clothes: the cutting tone, the sarcasm, the constant criticism that is never satisfied, the contempt, the short temper, the silence used as a weapon, the “winning” of every argument by sheer sharpness. Often it is the strange sin of the man who is gentle and pleasant with everyone — colleagues, friends, strangers — and saves his harshness for his own wife. The cure is the very character Paul has just commanded: the compassion, kindness, meekness, and patience of 3:12, and the readiness to forgive rather than to nurse a grievance until it sours (3:13). Where love would cherish, harshness wounds; and a wife was never given to her husband to be a target for his bitterness, but to be loved as Christ loves. cf. Eph. 5:25–29; 1 Pet. 3:7.

verseByVerse.quote: Children, obey your parents in everything, for this pleases the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Children, obey your parents” — and how this looks changes with the years. Notice first that Paul speaks directly to the children — they are real members of the church, able to hear God’s word and answer it. “Obey” means to listen and to do — not merely to feel respect but actively to heed. And this looks different at different ages. For the young child, it is plain, glad, prompt obedience in the daily round — coming when called, doing the chore, going to bed, minding mum and dad; this is the very nursery of discipleship, where a little one first learns to submit to God by submitting to those God has set over him. For the older child and teenager, the relationship matures but the call remains: obedience now expressed as honour and trust — keeping the household’s rules, receiving correction and guidance without rebellion, trusting a parent’s wisdom even when it chafes. And for the grown child who has left home and formed his own household, the word shifts: the duty to obey belongs to the years under the parental roof, but the duty to honour never expires. “Honour your father and mother” (Eph. 6:2) is for life — the adult child no longer takes orders as a boy did, but he never stops respecting, listening to, caring for, and providing for his parents as they age (1 Tim. 5:4, 8). Obedience belongs to childhood; honour is lifelong.

One needful word on “in everything.” The sweep is wide — the whole ordinary life of the home — but it is not absolute, for all human authority is held under God’s. The parallel reads “obey your parents in the Lord” (Eph. 6:1). A child is never bound to obey a parent who commands him to sin against God, for then the higher authority must be obeyed (Acts 5:29). But that exception is rare; the plain meaning, for nearly every child on nearly every day, is simply this: obey, fully and gladly.

“For this pleases the Lord” — why does it delight him so? Above all, because in obeying, a child walks in the very footsteps of the Lord Jesus himself. For Christ is the great obedient Son: “I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38); “I always do the things that are pleasing to him” (John 8:29); he was “obedient to the point of death” (Phil. 2:8). And here is the wonder — the eternal Son, the One by whom all things were made, spent thirty years in a carpenter’s home and “was submissive” to Mary and Joseph (Luke 2:51). The Lord of glory obeyed his earthly parents in Nazareth. So when a child obeys, he is bearing the family likeness of the Son who delighted to obey his Father — and that is a thing of beauty to God. Two other reasons join it. The obedient home reflects God’s own good order, the design by which he made the world to run on glad, ordered love. And the child’s obedience to his parents is, underneath, obedience to God, who set parents over him; to honour the authority God established is to honour God. Let a child hear it plainly: when you obey, you genuinely bring joy to the heart of God — and you do it not to win his love, but as one who already belongs to the obedient Son. cf. Prov. 1:8–9; Luke 2:51–52.

verseByVerse.quote: Fathers, do not provoke your children, lest they become discouraged.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Fathers, do not provoke your children” — what is being forbidden? The word means to irritate, exasperate, stir up to resentment. The parallel puts it sharply: “do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord” (Eph. 6:4). So here, as with the husband and the master, the one who holds the power is the one given the restraining word: a father’s strength is to build his children up, never to crush them. Fathers exasperate their children in a hundred ways — by harshness and a never-satisfied criticism, by unfairness and favouritism, by punishing in temper, by impossible expectations, by domineering control, by hypocrisy (demanding what he will not do himself), and by cold neglect that withholds all warmth and praise. The good way is the opposite of every one of these: patient, warm, consistent nurture that disciplines and encourages, and that points the child to Christ. It is worth seeing how this looks across the years.

The young child. A father provokes a little one by impatience and a sharp tongue over ordinary childish failings — the spilled cup, the slowness, the mess — by anger out of all proportion, by rules that change with his mood, by promises lightly broken, by expecting a small child to behave like an adult. The good way is gentleness and patience: clear, consistent boundaries held with warmth, getting down to the child’s level, generous affection and praise, expectations fitted to his age, and promises kept. And when a young child is provoked, the discouragement shows plainly — in tears and flinching, in a new timidity or clinginess, in a once-bright spark gone anxious and withdrawn. A little heart bruises easily.

The school-age child. Here a father provokes by constant criticism of schoolwork and chores, by comparing the child to a sibling or a classmate, by praise that never comes, by mockery and sarcasm, by overreacting to mistakes, by shaming him in front of others, by demanding a perfection no child can reach. The good way is to encourage and to notice — specific praise for honest effort, real interest in the child’s world (his games, his friends, the things he is proud of), discipline that is fair and explained rather than arbitrary, patient instruction, time and attention freely given. The discouraged school-age child gives up trying (“why bother — I’ll never be good enough for him”), grows sullen, begins to lie to dodge the criticism, and quietly stops bringing his small joys to his father at all.

The teenager. A father provokes a teen by clamping down with a control that will not loosen as the child grows, by still treating him as a little boy, by extending no trust and no freedom, by endless lecturing, by belittling his opinions or his appearance, by “because I said so” where a reason was owed, by hypocrisy, and by refusing ever to listen. The good way is to let trust and responsibility grow together, to listen to and respect a developing mind, to reason rather than merely command, to choose the battles that matter and let the rest go, to keep the relationship warm, to model integrity and even to own his own faults — and above all to point the young person to Christ, not merely to enforce a rulebook. When a teen is provoked, the discouragement runs deep: it erupts as open rebellion and bitterness, or — just as dangerous — it sinks inward into withdrawal, secrecy, a shut door, a deadened and joyless compliance, the look of a young heart that has quietly given up on its father.

The grown child — and the Father behind all fathers. Even a grown child can be provoked: by a father who still dictates, who criticises his choices, his spouse, or his way of raising his own children, who withholds approval to the end. The good way now is to honour the child’s adulthood — to advise when asked, to bless rather than control — and the provoked adult child shows his discouragement by distance, avoidance, and a quiet, weary keeping away. Through every stage one pattern holds, and it is the gospel that sets it: the earthly father is to father as God fathers his own — “as a father shows compassion to his children, so the LORD shows compassion to those who fear him” (Ps. 103:13). God disciplines, but he never crushes; he is firm, yet tender; he is the Father from whom all fatherhood takes its name (Eph. 3:14–15). And the Christian father parents not to earn anything, but out of the fullness of a man who is himself a dearly loved child of that Father — passing on to his children the very grace he has received. cf. Eph. 6:4; Heb. 12:7–11.

verseByVerse.quote: Bondservants, obey in everything those who are your earthly masters, not by way of eye-service, as people-pleasers, but with sincerity of heart, fearing the Lord. Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward. You are serving the Lord Christ. For the wrongdoer will be paid back for the wrong he has done, and there is no partiality.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What was a “bondservant”? The word is doulos, slave. Slavery ran right through the Roman world — perhaps a third of the empire — but it was not the race-based chattel slavery of later centuries. People became slaves by capture in war, by birth to a slave mother, or by selling themselves to escape debt and poverty. A slave was legally his master’s property, owing labour and obedience; yet many were educated — doctors, teachers, estate managers — could hold some money of their own, and could in time be freed by their master or buy their own freedom. So it was a harsh and varied institution, not a permanent doom. (Paul is not blessing the system; elsewhere he quietly undermines it — “if you can gain your freedom, do so,” 1 Cor. 7:21; and in Christ master and slave are brothers, Philemon. He is teaching believers how to live for Christ inside a system the gospel would in time dissolve.) The parallel to the modern employee is real but partial: like the worker today, the slave laboured under another’s authority and owed honest work — but unlike him, the slave was owned, unpaid, and often without choice or exit. So the how-to-work of these verses carries straight across to any job; the conditions do not.

“Obey in everything those who are your earthly masters” — the command. “In everything” means the full scope of the master’s lawful direction — the whole task, not just the pleasant parts, done thoroughly and without shirking (with the same unspoken limit that governs all such obedience: never into sin, for the Lord outranks every master). And mark the exact phrase: “earthly masters” is literally “masters according to the flesh.” In a single phrase Paul has already put the human master in his place — he is your master only on the earthly, passing level; you have another and greater Master above him.

“Not by way of eye-service, as people-pleasers” — then and now. “Eye-service” (a word Paul seems to have coined) is work that only happens while the master’s eye is on you — busy when watched, idle when his back is turned. The “people-pleaser” works to impress the man, to win approval or dodge punishment, putting on a show. It is one of the oldest temptations of the workplace, and it has not aged a day: the employee who looks busy when the manager passes and slacks when he is gone, who games the metrics and polishes appearances for the review, who gives the minimum that will not get him caught. The gospel has no room for “as long as nobody is looking” — because Someone always is.

“But with sincerity of heart, fearing the Lord” — the new motive. Against all that, an undivided, genuine heart — the same whether watched or not — and a reverent “fear of the Lord.” Here is the great turn, and it is exactly as it sounds: you work well not because the master deserves it, not because he happens to be watching, but because you stand in awe of the Lord who is always watching and whose will this is. Even a slave with a cruel and thankless master serves with all his heart — not for the master’s sake at all, but for the Lord’s. The audience of your work has changed: it is no longer the boss; it is God.

“Whatever you do, work heartily”. The Greek is vivid: work “from the soul” — put your whole self into it, with energy and goodwill, not grudgingly or by halves. And “whatever you do” spares nothing from this — the menial task, the unseen task, the dreary task: stack the shelf, sweep the floor, fill in the form — from the soul.

“As for the Lord and not for men” — the principle that changes everything. Here is why drudgery becomes worship. You are not, in the end, working for the man who signs your orders; you are working for the Lord. Christ is your true Master, and every task is handed, as it were, directly to him. The earthly master may be unworthy, ungrateful, even cruel — it does not finally matter, because he is not the one you are ultimately serving. Hand the swept floor to Jesus, and a mean master cannot rob it of its glory (cf. Eph. 6:7; Col. 3:17).

“Knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward”. Now feel the force of this. Under Roman law a slave could not inherit — inheritances went to sons and heirs, never to slaves. Yet Paul promises this slave the inheritance — the whole eternal estate of God’s people (1:12), “imperishable…kept in heaven for you” (1 Pet. 1:4). The man who owns nothing and can inherit nothing on earth is a full heir of God. And see how the argument presses the command: the slave may get no wage, no thanks, no advancement from his earthly master — but the Lord sees, and will repay, not with coins but with glory. So serve heartily, with your eyes lifted past the thankless present to the certain reward. (Note: the inheritance is not wages earned — you receive it as a son, by grace; the “reward” is God graciously crowning the very service his own grace enabled.)

“You are serving the Lord Christ” — in what way? This is the clincher. When the believing slave does his master’s bidding, he is in reality rendering that service to Christ — it is Christ who receives it, Christ who is truly being served. The lowliest labour, done in faith, rises to the King of kings as service offered to him (cf. Matt. 25:40). So the slave is not merely the slave of some human master; he is, in the deepest truth of it, a servant of the Lord Christ — and there is no higher title in all the universe.

“The wrongdoer will be paid back…and there is no partiality” — who is warned? The word can reach both ways, and is meant to. To the slave it is a warning: do not imagine your low place lets you get away with lazy, dishonest, or spiteful work — “my master mistreats me, so I will cheat him” — for God repays wrong even in a slave. To the master it is a threat (the very next verse, 4:1, turns to address him): the master who wrongs his servant will not escape. The hinge is the last phrase — “there is no partiality.” God plays no favourites; he weighs the deed, not the rank. The Judge is not impressed by a master’s wealth nor dismissive of a slave’s lowliness. So the powerless need not fear that the powerful will buy their way out: every wrong will be repaid, by the Lord himself, at his judgment, with perfect even-handedness. cf. Rom. 2:11; Acts 10:34.

Now bring it into Old Joe’s world — and behold the beauty of it. Old Joe is no slave, but he has a boss, a job, and a great heap of work that is repetitive, unseen, and rarely thanked. Watch what this passage does to his Monday. The cleaner mopping an empty corridor, the clerk filling the same forms, the carer washing a body no one else will touch — when it is done “for the Lord,” it is laid into the hands of the King who flung the stars into space and bled upon a cross. His foreman may never say thank you; the Lord is keeping account, and forgets nothing. No task is too small to be worship, no worker too low to be Christ’s honoured servant, no good hour ever truly unseen. And here is the wonder that should raise the hair on the back of the neck: the slave who owns nothing, who can inherit nothing, who is invisible to the great of this world — he is the servant of the Lord Christ and the heir of all things. The drudgery turns to glory; the overlooked man is the honoured one; the dreary shift becomes the very stuff of eternity. And Old Joe does none of this to earn Christ — he is already his, already an heir — but as a beloved son carrying his clumsy day’s work up to a Father who is delighted to receive it. Whatever you do, Old Joe — do it for him. cf. 1 Cor. 15:58.

4.title: Devoted to Prayer: Wisdom, Words, and the Gospel Network
4.overview:
The final chapter of Colossians is shorter and more personal than the preceding chapters but carries the letter’s theology into two final areas: the Christian’s relationship to prayer and to the world (vv. 2–6), and the network of relationships through which the gospel advances (vv. 7–18). Together they show the gospel in its two directions: upward (prayer) and outward (mission), and the community of people in whom those directions are embodied.

The instructions on prayer and conduct (vv. 2–6) are brief but theologically dense. Prayer requires steadfastness and watchfulness — active, alert engagement rather than routine. Thanksgiving is its constant accompaniment. The prayer for open doors for the word of the mystery of Christ — the mystery Paul himself is imprisoned for proclaiming — is the prayer of a man for whom the gospel’s advance is more important than his own comfort or release. Conduct toward outsiders is to be “in wisdom,” making the best use of the time, with speech that is “gracious, seasoned with salt” — the attractive, preserving, flavour-giving quality that makes the gospel winsome as well as true.

The closing personal greetings reveal the extraordinary network of relationships through which the gospel was advancing in the first century: Tychicus, Onesimus, Aristarchus, Mark (the John Mark of Acts 15, apparently reconciled with Paul), Justus, Epaphras, Luke, Demas, Nympha and her house church, Archippus. These are not decorative biographical details; they are the human face of the gospel’s advance, the community of grace in its concrete, particular, named reality.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul’s closing instructions begin where the new life always begins — on its knees. “Continue steadfastly in prayer,” he says, and the very command is a comfort, for he would not have to urge perseverance if prayer were easy to sustain. Three notes mark the praying he calls for: it is to be steadfast (dogged and persevering, not occasional), watchful (awake and alert, the sentry who will not doze, never a drowsy mumble), and thankful (saturated with gratitude, which guards prayer from collapsing into a mere list of wants and fuels the very perseverance he has just commanded). A church that prays like this will not easily be carried off by any false teacher.

Then comes the request that startles — for it comes from a man in chains. Paul asks not for the prison door to open but for “a door for the word”: his concern is not his own freedom but the gospel’s. And he, the great apostle, asks a church he has never met to pray for him — proof that none of us, however gifted, outgrows the need of God’s help and his people’s prayers. He longs to declare “the mystery of Christ” — the long-hidden, now-revealed secret who is a Person — and even prays for the plain clarity of his own preaching, presuming nothing on his eloquence. And he names the cause of his imprisonment without a breath of complaint against Rome or against God: he is simply the prisoner of Christ Jesus, resting in the sovereign hand that set him there for the gospel’s advance.

From the church’s prayer Paul turns to its public face before the watching world. Believers are to “walk in wisdom toward outsiders” — living with such integrity and winsomeness that their conduct adorns the gospel rather than repelling people from it, avoiding both compromise with the world and a sour, superior aloofness from it. They are to be “making the best use of the time” — buying up every fleeting opportunity, as a shrewd merchant snaps up a bargain, to do good and to point to Christ before the moment passes. And their speech is to be “gracious, seasoned with salt” — kind and flavourful, winsome and wholesome, neither bland nor cutting — so that they are ready to give a fitting, tailored answer to each person who asks about the hope that is in them. Wise conduct and gracious speech are how a church wins a hearing for the gospel it prays God to advance.
verseByVerse.theology:
Prayer as Steadfast Engagement, Not Occasional Request

Paul’s instruction to “continue steadfastly in prayer” (proskartereite) reflects the Reformed conviction that prayer is not an emergency resort but the fundamental posture of the creature before the Creator. The same verb is used in Acts 1:14 of the disciples’ prayer in the upper room and in Acts 2:42 of the early church’s corporate life. Steadfast prayer is the mark of a community that has genuinely reckoned with its dependence on God and genuinely believes that prayer moves the hands that move the world.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul, in prison, could not personally open the doors for the gospel’s advance. He could pray — and he could enlist the Colossians to pray with him. The prayer for open doors is the prayer of the person who has surrendered control of the gospel’s advance to the one who actually controls it. Now: The church that wants to reach the lost but neglects corporate prayer has misunderstood the mechanism by which God works. Open doors are God’s to give; prayer is the community’s engagement with the God who gives them.

verseByVerse.quote: Masters, treat your bondservants justly and fairly, knowing that you also have a Master in heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Masters” — who were they, and what is the bridge to today? The word is kyrioi — the very same word as “Lord.” In the Roman world a master held near-absolute power over his slaves: he could command, punish, sell, and (in law) even kill them, with little or no accountability. A slave was reckoned property — Aristotle had called him “a living tool” — an economic asset valued for what he produced, not a person with rights. The duties of the household ran one way only, from slave up to master; almost no one thought a master owed his slaves anything. That is what makes this verse quietly revolutionary: Paul turns and addresses the masters, and lays an obligation on them. The bridge to our world is the employer — the boss, the manager, the business owner, the executive, anyone who holds power over other people’s work and livelihood. The old temptation survives intact: to see workers as “resources” (we even say human resources), units of production, replaceable cogs valued only for their output and the bottom line. To every Christian who holds such power, this verse speaks directly.

“Treat your bondservants justly and fairly”. Two words carry it. “Justly” means to render what is right and due — honest dealing, what is owed, fair provision, discipline that is just and not cruel or arbitrary. “Fairly” is literally equality, equity — even-handed, impartial treatment, with a hint of the deeper truth that in Christ this slave is in fact your equal and your brother. A standard like this went far beyond anything Roman law asked of a slaveowner: the one-way street becomes two-way, and the slave is suddenly a person to whom justice is owed. Picture it concretely — a Christian master in Colossae (think of Philemon) told to deal righteously with his slaves, even to welcome a runaway back as a “beloved brother” (Philem. 16). And bring it into the corporate world: the Christian employer owes his people a fair wage (not squeezing labour while profits soar), honest contracts kept, safe conditions, reasonable demands, no favouritism, no exploitation, no treating human beings as disposable. It looks like the owner who shares the gain fairly, the manager who disciplines by principle rather than by mood, the executive who will not cut the corner that harms his workers, the boss who treats the night cleaner and the senior partner with the same human dignity. The Christian in authority should be the most just and humane employer in town.

“Knowing that you also have a Master in heaven” — how the argument works. Here is the whole motive, and it is a master-stroke of wording: the master (kyrios) is told he has a Master (Kyrios). The man who holds the power is himself a servant; over the one who stands at the top of the earthly ladder stands One who owns him utterly. So Paul levels the hierarchy not by abolishing it but by pointing straight up: deal justly with those beneath you, because you will answer for it to the Lord above you — the same Lord who, he has just said, “shows no partiality” (3:25). The master’s wealth and rank buy him nothing at that throne; his Lord is watching how he treats the people in his power, and will repay. And there is a humbling sweetness folded in: master and slave have the same Master in heaven — they kneel side by side at one throne, equals before the God who made and bought them both. The cross levels everyone; at its foot the boss and the worker are two sinners saved by the same grace. The Christian who holds authority, then, wields it not as a little lord but as a fellow-servant who never forgets the Master over his own shoulder. cf. Eph. 6:9; Lev. 25:43; Job 31:13–15.

verseByVerse.quote: Continue steadfastly in prayer, being watchful in it with thanksgiving.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Continue steadfastly in prayer” — and notice that we are told to. The word means to persevere, to hold fast, to stick doggedly at a thing and not give it up — the same word used of the first church, who “devoted themselves” to prayer (Acts 2:42). And the very fact that Paul must command it tells us something tender and true: staying steadfast in prayer is hard, and we need the encouragement. Why is it so hard? Because prayer is hidden, unseen labour with no visible machinery; because answers often tarry and we grow discouraged; because the flesh is weak and prayer can feel like “doing nothing”; because we are busy, distracted, and easily dried up; and because there is an enemy who would far rather we did anything than pray. So Paul does not say “pray when you feel like it” but “keep at it” — persevere. It was for exactly this that Jesus told the parable of the persistent widow, “that they ought always to pray and not lose heart” (Luke 18:1). Do not measure your praying by how it feels; simply do not stop. Every lapse is to be followed by a return; the goal is not perfect prayer but persistent prayer.

“Being watchful in it” — what did Paul mean? The word means to stay awake, alert, on guard — the picture is the sentry on night watch who dare not doze. It carries the memory of Gethsemane, where the Lord found his disciples asleep and said, “Watch and pray” (Matt. 26:41). To be watchful in prayer is, first, to pray awake — mind genuinely present, not a drowsy, mechanical mumble with a wandering heart. It is, second, to pray with open eyes — alert to what actually needs praying for (in your life, the church, the world) and expectant for God’s answer, like a watchman looking for the dawn. And it is, third, to be vigilant — for prayer’s great enemy is not so much hostility as drowsiness, the dull, half-asleep going-through-the-motions that empties prayer of life. Come awake, pay attention, mean it, and watch for God to act.

“With thanksgiving” — the indispensable companion. For the fifth time in this short letter, Paul sounds the note of thanks (1:12; 2:7; 3:15–17; here) — now woven right into prayer. Why does it matter so? Because thanksgiving keeps prayer from collapsing into a mere list of demands and complaints; it lifts the eyes from what we lack to all that God has already given. And that backward look fuels the perseverance Paul has just commanded — remembering yesterday’s mercies steadies the heart to keep asking today. The grateful pray-er is the persevering pray-er: thanksgiving crowds out the grumbling and discouragement that make us quietly give prayer up. And it is only fitting, for we come not to wring favours from a reluctant stranger but as children to a Father who has already given us his Son — so we ask with thanks already on our lips (cf. Phil. 4:6).

verseByVerse.quote: At the same time, pray also for us, that God may open to us a door for the word, to declare the mystery of Christ, on account of which I am in prison — that I may make it clear, which is how I ought to speak.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Pray also for us” — even Paul asked for prayer. Stop and feel the weight of this. Paul — the apostle chosen by the risen Christ, caught up to the third heaven, a writer of Scripture, the planter of churches across the empire — turns to a small congregation he has never even met and asks them to pray for him. The greatest Christian of the age leaning on the prayers of ordinary, faraway believers. The lesson is plain and humbling: even the best, the most gifted, the most mature of us never outgrows his need of God’s help and of his brothers’ prayers. If Paul needed praying for, how much more do we — and how much more should we pray for one another, for our pastors, our missionaries, our struggling friends. And it cuts the other way too: the humblest saint’s prayers truly count, for the prayers of this little church could shape the ministry of an apostle. Old Joe’s prayers for his pastor are no formality; they move the hand that moves the world. (Paul asks this everywhere — Rom. 15:30; Eph. 6:19; 1 Thess. 5:25.)

“That God may open to us a door for the word”. The “open door” is Paul’s picture for a God-given opportunity to preach (1 Cor. 16:9; 2 Cor. 2:12). And mark two things. First, it is God who opens it — the apostle can only walk through the doors the Lord swings open; even the chance to share Christ is a gift of God’s providence, not the fruit of our cleverness. Second, and tenderly: a man in chains does not ask for the prison door to open — he asks for a door for the word. His own freedom is not his concern; the gospel’s freedom is. “I am bound with chains,” he wrote, “but the word of God is not bound” (2 Tim. 2:9). So pray for open doors — for gospel workers and for yourself — remembering that it is God who opens them.

“To declare the mystery of Christ” — why “mystery,” and not simply “the gospel”? It is the same good news, but Paul chooses the richer word on purpose. A “mystery” in his vocabulary (see 1:26–27) is a secret long hidden in the heart of God and now thrown open — here, the staggering plan that Christ would dwell in his people and be proclaimed to all the nations, Jew and Gentile alike. So “mystery of Christ” frames the gospel as God’s eternal, once-concealed purpose at last unveiled — and it presses the point that this mystery is not a system or a secret technique (as the false teachers offered their initiates) but a Person: “God’s mystery, which is Christ” (2:2). Paul does not preach a thing; he declares a Someone — the One in whom all God’s hidden purpose is summed up and revealed.

“On account of which I am in prison” — and not a word of complaint. Here is one of the quiet wonders of this letter. Paul names the reason for his chains plainly and without a trace of grumbling — not against Rome, not against his accusers, not against God, and not a breath of self-pity. He simply states the root cause: he is in prison for the mystery of Christ. He does not see himself as a victim of Roman injustice or of bad luck; he looks straight past the magistrates and the soldiers to the sovereign hand behind them, and calls himself not the prisoner of Caesar but “the prisoner of Christ Jesus” (Eph. 3:1; Philem. 1). He so believed in the reign of God that he could write, from a cell, “what has happened to me has really served to advance the gospel” (Phil. 1:12). A man unjustly bound, who might have raged or despaired, instead owns his chains as Christ’s service, asks not for release but for open doors, and rests in the God who set him there for a purpose. That is what it looks like to truly believe God is sovereign — peace where there might have been bitterness, purpose where there might have been despair. And it searches us: what do we do with our own “prisons” — the unjust treatment, the shut door, the hard providence? Grumble at people and at God, or trust the sovereign hand and ask how Christ might be made known even here?

“That I may make it clear, which is how I ought to speak” — even Paul needed help with his words. Notice that his request is not only for an open door but for a clear word — that when he speaks he will make the mystery plain, as he is bound to. And there is great humility in it: the most gifted preacher and writer the church has ever known does not presume on his own eloquence; he asks for prayer that he might speak clearly, as he ought. An open door is wasted without a clear message on the far side of it. If Paul leaned on God and on the prayers of others for the very clarity of his speech, then so must we — whenever we share Christ with a neighbour, teach a class, or simply try to explain the hope that is in us, we need God to give us the words and to make them clear. Pray it for your preachers; pray it for yourself. cf. Eph. 6:19–20; Col. 4:6.

verseByVerse.quote: Walk in wisdom toward outsiders, making the best use of the time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A new subject — or is it? Paul has just asked them to pray for his witness, that God would open a door for the word (vv. 3–4); now he turns to their witness — how the church itself is to commend Christ to “outsiders.” The two belong together: pray for the gospel’s advance, and live so as to advance it. And this is no abrupt change of subject but the natural outward movement of the whole letter. Paul has set forth the supremacy and all-sufficiency of Christ (chs. 1–2), the new life that flows from being raised with him (ch. 3), the transformed home (3:18–4:1), and devoted prayer (4:2–4) — and now that new life must show its face to the watching world. The Christ who has filled them is meant to overflow toward those who do not yet know him. “Outsiders” (literally those outside) are the non-Christians among whom they live, and Paul cares greatly how the church appears to them, for the world reads the gospel first in the lives of those who profess it.

“Walk in wisdom toward outsiders” — what it looks like. “Walk” is the whole conduct of life; “in wisdom” means with the skill, discernment, and tact of the wisdom that is hidden in Christ (2:3) — knowing how to live before non-Christians in a way that adorns the gospel rather than repelling people from it. The watching world either sees something in a believer that draws it toward Christ, or something that slams the door. So it looks like integrity — honest in business, reliable in your word; like genuine kindness and being a good neighbour; like a blameless life that disarms criticism (1 Pet. 2:12); and like the tact to know when to speak and when to stay quiet. It avoids two ditches at once: compromise (simply blending into the world) and harsh superiority (the sour, judgmental believer the world rightly recoils from). The only offence we should ever give is the offence of the gospel itself — never the offence of our rudeness, hypocrisy, or foolishness. In a pagan town like Colossae it meant the Christian who was honest in the market and faithful to his word, who would not join the drunken excess of the temple feasts and yet was no sneering prig — so that his neighbours saw something different and winsome. Today it is the believer at work who is diligent and will not gossip or cut corners, the neighbour quick to help, the Christian online who does not meet every quarrel with cruelty — the one whose ordinary integrity makes the gospel believable. Old Joe’s daily conduct before his unbelieving workmates is itself either an argument for Christ or against him.

“Making the best use of the time” — then and now. The phrase is vivid: literally, “buying up the opportunity” — and the word for time is not the ticking clock (chronos) but the opportune moment (kairos), the open window. The picture is a shrewd merchant snapping up a bargain before it is gone. For Paul, in this setting, it means seizing every God-given opening to commend Christ — every chance to do good and to point to the Saviour — before it passes; the parallel adds the reason, “because the days are evil” (Eph. 5:16). The believer redeems the very time the world squanders. And so today: opportunities are fleeting and life is short, so make the most of every encounter — the colleague going through a hard season, the unexpected question about your hope, the moment to help or to speak a word for Christ. That open window with this neighbour or that relative may not come again; buy it up. Treat each ordinary day as a satchel of God-given opportunities to be redeemed, not frittered away.

verseByVerse.quote: Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt” — what does this mean? Note first the sweep: always — all your talk, not merely your “religious” talk. Two qualities are to mark it. “Gracious” (literally, “with grace”) means speech that is kind, winsome, and pleasant — and more, speech that actually gives grace to those who hear it (Eph. 4:29), as the “gracious words” that fell from the lips of Jesus drew the crowds (Luke 4:22). “Seasoned with salt” draws on what salt did: it gave food flavour and kept it from spoiling. So salted speech is not bland, insipid, dreary talk, but speech with savour, interest, wit, and substance — worth listening to — and wholesome, free of what is corrupt or coarse. (Note that this is the very opposite of the modern sense of “salty” speech, which is crude; Paul means tasteful and lively, not foul.)

Hold the two together and you see the balance. Speech that is gracious but not salted is kind but bland — mushy, gushing, saying nothing memorable. Speech that is salted but not gracious is clever but cruel, witty but cutting, sharp at another’s expense. The Christian’s tongue is to be both at once: kind and interesting, warm and with bite, truthful and winsome — just as the Lord himself spoke words that drew people in yet carried point and edge and stayed in the memory. In practice it is answering a hostile remark with unexpected kindness rather than defensiveness; speaking a hard truth seasoned so that it can be heard rather than blurted to wound; trading the coarse joke and the sour complaint for words that leave a good taste and build people up. Let Old Joe’s talk at the workbench and the kitchen table be neither sour and harsh nor limp and dull, but gracious words with a wholesome tang that make people glad to listen.

“So that you may know how you ought to answer each person” — ready for whom, and for what? Here is the aim of all that gracious, salted speech: to be ready to give a fitting reply to each one who asks. Mark the words “each person” — not a single canned formula fired off at everyone, but an answer suited to this individual, his question, his need, his objection; the same wisdom toward outsiders that v. 5 called for, now in conversation. And what sort of questions? In this setting, the questions of the watching world about the faith — “why do you live like that?”, “why are you so hopeful?”, the honest enquiry, the sceptic’s challenge, the objection thrown down. Peter says the same: “always be prepared to make a defence to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you, yet with gentleness and respect” (1 Pet. 3:15). And see how the verse hangs together: gracious, flavourful speech is the soil, and readiness to answer is the fruit. A believer whose everyday words are winsome and wholesome will draw people to ask — and be ready, when they do, to answer that particular person well; whereas harsh or insipid talk shuts the conversation before it can begin. So Old Joe need not have a sermon by heart; he needs a gracious, salted tongue and a heart ready to give this workmate a wise, kind, fitting word about the hope that is in him. cf. 1 Pet. 3:15; Prov. 15:23.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The letter ends not with a flourish of doctrine but with a page of names — and a modern reader must not skim them, for this closing roll-call is the gospel in its concrete, human form. Here is a living network of real people bound together by Christ, and the words Paul keeps reaching for tell the story: “beloved brother,” “faithful minister,” “fellow servant,” “fellow prisoner,” “a comfort to me.” And look who stands in the circle: Jews and Gentiles in one mission, Luke the educated physician beside Onesimus the runaway slave, Nympha the woman with a whole church in her house. The very walls Paul said Christ had thrown down (3:11) lie flat before our eyes; “Christ is all, and in all” has come all the way down to a list of friends.

Two names make the heart swell. Onesimus, the runaway slave, is sent home not as a criminal but as “our faithful and beloved brother” — the Roman social order quietly overturned in a phrase. And Mark, who once abandoned Paul mid-mission and split him from Barnabas, is here restored and welcomed — grace does not discard those who fail, it remakes them. (A sober shadow falls too: Demas, named here among the faithful, will one day desert for love of this present world.) At the centre kneels Epaphras, the church’s founder, “always struggling” in prayer — the athlete’s straining word — that they would “stand mature and fully assured in all the will of God,” which is the whole letter distilled into a single petition. These are Paul’s “fellow workers for the kingdom of God” — the kingdom into which, this very letter has said, believers have already been transferred (1:13), and for whose advance they now labour as they await its coming in glory.

Then the apostle takes the pen from his secretary’s hand: “I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand.” It is at once a seal of the letter’s genuineness and a touch of pure affection — and then, in his own script, “Remember my chains.” The whole soaring letter on the supremacy of Christ was written by a prisoner, and the chains are themselves an argument, for no one wears irons for a lie. And the last word answers the first: the letter that opened “grace to you” (1:2) closes “grace be with you.” To a church tempted to climb to God by rules and secret knowledge, the final word is the first word — grace, from beginning to end, all the way home.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Community of the Gospel as the Body of Christ

The list of names at the end of Colossians is the practical expression of the ecclesiology of 1:18: Christ is the head of the body, the church. The body is not an abstract entity; it is Tychicus and Onesimus and Luke and Nympha. The community of grace is always concrete, always named, always embodied in particular people with particular histories, gifts, and needs. Reformed ecclesiology has always insisted on the visible, particular, local church as the primary form of the body of Christ: not an ideal church somewhere, but this church, these people, this place, this time.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Onesimus is the most striking name on the list. The runaway slave, the subject of the letter to Philemon, is now a “faithful and beloved brother” being commended to the Colossians. The gospel has done exactly what Paul said it would do in 3:11: it has abolished the slave/free distinction as a defining category. Onesimus and Philemon are brothers; Onesimus and the Colossians are family. Now: The community of the gospel is always the community of the surprising, the reconciled, the transformed. The people who would never have been in the same room together are gathered at the same table because Christ is all, and in all.

verseByVerse.quote: Tychicus will tell you all about my activities. He is a beloved brother and faithful minister and fellow servant in the Lord. I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know how we are and that he may encourage your hearts, and with him Onesimus, our faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you. They will tell you of everything that has taken place here. Aristarchus my fellow prisoner greets you, and Mark the cousin of Barnabas (concerning whom you have received instructions—if he comes to you, welcome him), and Jesus who is called Justus. These are the only men of the circumcision among my fellow workers for the kingdom of God, and they have been a comfort to me. Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ Jesus, greets you, always struggling on your behalf in his prayers, that you may stand mature and fully assured in all the will of God. For I bear him witness that he has worked hard for you and for those in Laodicea and in Hierapolis. Luke the beloved physician greets you, as does Demas. Give my greetings to the brothers at Laodicea, and to Nympha and the church in her house. And when this letter has been read among you, have it also read in the church of the Laodiceans; and see that you also read the letter from Laodicea. And say to Archippus, ‘See that you fulfill the ministry that you have received in the Lord.’ I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand. Remember my chains. Grace be with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not a throwaway list. A modern reader is tempted to skim a page of ancient names and greetings. Do not. This closing roll-call is a living photograph of the gospel at work — a network of real people bound together by Christ — and it quietly preaches everything the letter has argued. Listen to the words Paul keeps reaching for: “beloved brother,” “faithful minister,” “fellow servant,” “fellow prisoner,” “a comfort to me.” These are not office colleagues; they are family, sharing one mission, one suffering, one Lord. The gospel does not merely save individuals; it makes a people who love one another like this.

Every wall down — the gospel family on display. Look who is in this little circle, and feel the wonder of it. There are Jews — Aristarchus, Mark, Jesus called Justus, “the only men of the circumcision among my fellow workers” — and Gentiles, side by side in one mission. There is Luke, an educated physician, and there is Onesimus, a runaway slave. There is Nympha, a woman, with a whole church meeting in her house. Jew and Greek, slave and free, man and woman, learned and lowly — the very divisions Paul said Christ had abolished (3:11) are here dissolved before our eyes into one family. The doctrine of the great hymn has come all the way down to a list of friends: “Christ is all, and in all.”

Two trophies of grace. Two names especially make the heart swell. First, Onesimus — “our faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you.” This is the runaway slave of the letter to Philemon, and Paul sends him home not branded a criminal but publicly honoured as a beloved brother; the social order of the whole Roman world is quietly overturned in five words. Second, Mark — “if he comes to you, welcome him.” This is the young man who once abandoned Paul mid-mission and became the cause of a bitter split (Acts 13:13; 15:37–39); yet here he is, restored, commended, a fellow worker again — the deserter become useful (2 Tim. 4:11). Grace does not discard those who have failed; it restores them. (And a sober shadow falls across the brightness: Demas is named here among the faithful, yet years later — “Demas, in love with this present world, has deserted me” (2 Tim. 4:10). Not all who begin well finish well; let it make us watchful.)

“Always struggling on your behalf in his prayers” — and what he prayed. Epaphras, the man who first brought them the gospel (1:7), is far from home with Paul — and he is on his knees for them. The word is “struggling” (the language of an athlete straining, an agony of effort) — the same word Paul used of his own labour for them (2:1). Here is intercession as costly, wrestling love: a pastor agonizing in prayer for a flock he cannot reach. And mark the precise content of his prayer — “that you may stand mature and fully assured in all the will of God.” This is the whole letter in a single petition. “Stand” — firm and established, not shifted off Christ (2:6–7). “Mature” (teleioi) — complete, full-grown, the goal of 1:28; not the false teachers’ “advanced” elite, but the maturity of those already filled in Christ (2:10). “Fully assured” (peplērophorēmenoi) — carried to settled, unshakable conviction, no longer tossed about. And all of it “in all the will of God” — not in esoteric secrets, but resting in the whole will of God made known in his Son. That is what Epaphras wanted for them; it is what every faithful shepherd longs to see; it is what we should beg God for one another.

“Fellow workers for the kingdom of God” — is the kingdom for us? Some have noticed that Paul speaks of the “kingdom of God” far less often than Jesus did in the Gospels, and have concluded that the kingdom is not really the church’s present concern — that it belongs to Israel, or waits wholly in the future. There is a precious truth in that instinct, and it should be honoured: the kingdom in its full, visible glory is still to come, when Christ returns to reign — and believers who long for that coming reign are right to long for it. But notice what Paul actually writes here: he and his companions are, right now, “fellow workers for the kingdom of God.” The kingdom is something they labour for in the present age. And earlier in this very letter Paul said something even more startling: God “has transferred us into the kingdom of his beloved Son” (1:13) — not will transfer, but has. So Scripture holds two truths together, and we must drop neither: the kingdom is already here, inaugurated wherever Christ is owned as King — we have already been brought into it — and it is not yet consummated, awaiting the King’s return in glory. The kingdom is most certainly “for us”: we already live in it, and we labour for its advance, even as we wait for its dawning in full. (That the word appears less often in the letters does not make the reality absent — Paul more often names it “union with Christ,” being “in him” — but the King and his reign are everywhere.) cf. Col. 1:13; Rom. 14:17; Acts 28:31.

“I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand. Remember my chains. Grace be with you.” Paul dictated his letters to a secretary (it was Tertius who penned Romans, Rom. 16:22), but at the close he takes the pen himself. Why? Partly to authenticate it — his own handwriting was the seal of genuineness, his guarantee that the letter was truly his (2 Thess. 3:17) — and partly for sheer affection, the apostle’s own hand reaching across the miles to touch them. Then picture it: a manacled hand taking the pen and scrawling, “Remember my chains.” The whole soaring letter about the supremacy and all-sufficiency of Christ was written by a prisoner — and the chains are themselves an argument, for no man wears irons for a lie. And then the last word. The letter that opened with “grace to you” (1:2) closes with “grace be with you.” To a church tempted to climb to God by rules and rituals and secret knowledge, the final word is the first word: grace — the free, inexhaustible, sovereign gift of God in the Christ in whom the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily, and in whom they have been filled. From grace, to grace, all the way home.
